The Big Picture · Field Guide

A personal operating system for the builder-leader

Personal agents are easy. The wall is team & company. This is the system that gets you across.

Read the canvas as a map; read this as the field guide. Each pattern is a recurring situation welded to the move that resolves it — Use when · Core moves · Build · Test · Why — sequenced along the value cycle: Intent → Context & Guardrails → The Work → Verification → Absorption → Outcome, looping back as the level rises from personal to team to company. Two lanes (software and business) grow in the same soil; where a move is genuinely the same, the cards say so.

Generated from the live pattern cards — a snapshot of a system still compounding.

Intent
Intent
Pattern · business lane · phase: Intent · the foundation node of the business mat

Train before you buy

The principle: clarity is the ceiling, not capability — you cannot design an organisation for a capability nobody in it understands.

Put the platform decision last, not first. Build a little competence inside the building before any vendor is in your calendar, and the unanswerable board question — "which platform?" — decomposes into three small, reversible ones. The repo's strategic frame, in order: competence → discovery → context → platform.

Same fork, two orders. On the dead path the platform is the first node; on the living one it's the last.
The mechanism · why the question is unanswerable first

Same board question, different answer — once competence exists.

Picture the room. Four horizontal platforms, five-plus vertical SaaS vendors, an open-source framework someone keeps championing, and roughly two hundred internal processes that might one day be agents. The board wants a recommendation by quarter-end. Every demo looks plausible; every evaluation is quietly shaped by whichever vendor presented last. The honest trouble isn't which platform — it's that nobody in the room can yet formulate the right question, because the right question only arrives once someone has actually built. The mental model is the missing input, and no slide supplies it.

This is structurally new. Past transformations — digital, agile, cloud — could be vision-led because the concepts were reachable by analogy: a CEO never wrote code, yet could picture a digital company. Agents break that. Say "an agent that processes invoices across three systems with human escalation at decision points" to someone who's never built or used one, and they hear "automation" and quietly file it under RPA. The gap isn't knowledge — it's experience, and you cannot brief your way across it. So the first move isn't a decision at all. It's a refusal: don't choose the platform yet.

The hardest problem isn't choosing a platform — it's knowing what questions to ask. Skip to platform selection and you're choosing between vendor narratives.

Process diagram · 01The big unanswerable question doesn't get answered — it gets decomposed. Competence is the only input that changed.

The traditional sequence runs assess → select platform → big procurement → 6-month pilot → maybe rollout. It feels responsible. It produces PowerPoints and vendor lock-in. The competence-first sequence inverts it: train people to build agents first, start with coding agents — the cheap, low-risk meta-platform — and let competence create the pull. People then discover their own high-value processes, and the infrastructure questions arrive scoped and answerable instead of abstract and board-sized. The consultancy default (assess → identify → build → train) is exactly backwards; competence-first flips it to train → identify → build → assess.

Notice the order has no shortcut around step one. One person builds something for themselves and gets the mental model. Personal use is the floor, not a warm-up — skip it and nothing above holds: no shared vision, no organisational learning, just a tidy procurement plan resting on an abstraction. And the people who've built are also your best surveyors. Builders find the gaps faster and more accurately than any consultancy assessment, and the gaps are predictable: three walls, every time — data access, somewhere to run what they build, and discoverability so others can find and reuse it. Those three are the real questions. Each is a lightweight two-way door.

The upgrade move · vendor narrative → builder evidence

From a procurement funnel to a pull engine.

The diagram below redraws the funnel as an engine. Same components, reversed wiring. The old funnel pours effort in at the top — assess, select, procure, pilot — and the platform decision sits at the very front, made by people who have watched demos. The pull engine starts with a tiny rep (train → build), lets discovery do the surveying, and defers the platform call to the very end, where it's now small, reversible, and run against your use cases rather than the vendor's reel. The person who's built one agent walks into the procurement meeting with evidence; everyone else walks in with narratives.

Process diagram · 02Same five stages, reversed wiring. Move the platform node from the front to the back and PowerPoints become questions worth answering.

Here's the part that makes it a foundation rather than a tactic. Competence doesn't just answer the platform question — it starts a chain. Competence creates mental models → mental models create shared vision → shared vision connects experiments → connected experiments become organisational learning → which pulls more people in to build. Each pass, the soil gets richer: a common language emerges, isolated wins start referencing each other, and the organisation can finally hold a coherent picture of what it's building toward. Skip the first link and the chain never forms — you get the HBR experimentation trap: hundreds of pilots that never connect, never scale, never compound.

You cannot design an organisation for a capability nobody in it understands. Build competence and the platform question shrinks from a board decision to a two-way door.

Process diagram · 03The loop closes without being a ring. Skip the entry node — personal use — and the whole chain above never forms.
The evidence · convergence, not proof

What the research actually says — caveats attached.

This is a convergence read, not a law. Several independent signals point the same way; each carries a caveat that must travel with it, because a number stripped of its genre is just a louder opinion. Read them as directional pressure, not measurement. The qualitative spine — the sequence, the mechanism, the field observation — is sturdier than any single statistic.

Cited evidence · directional · each line keeps its source genre
95%
of custom / task-specific GenAI tools reported no measurable P&L impact. MIT NANDA, Jul 2025 — N=52 interviews, a narrow P&L-impact definition, authors call it "directionally accurate"; NANDA also builds agent infrastructure (structural conflict of interest). Use directionally, never as "95% of AI projects fail."
8.6%
of companies have agents in production; 63.7% have no formalised AI initiative; 82% of early-maturity orgs have no talent strategy. Joget analyst aggregation — one analyst's roll-up of maturity data. Cite the source genre; don't launder these into established fact.
4%
of Nordic companies achieve strong AI returns; 58% expect 3+ years for significant ROI vs 37% in the rest of Europe. BCG Nordic 2026 / Deloitte Nordic Dec 2025 — two independent surveys (Level 3). The Nordic caution gap is the competence gap; do not call survey data "field evidence."
2–3x
productivity for individuals who build competence — yet orgs capture only 10–20%. The gap is shared mental models. Mollick / Wharton — research, directional. It's the mental-model-gap mechanism, not a guaranteed multiplier for any given org.
0
named companies found that succeeded with "buy platform first, train later" — across 63 research cycles and 18,500 Agentforce customers. repo OODA cycles · "What We Did Not Find" — a cited research absence: across 63 cycles we found none. Absence of evidence, stated as such — not a law that platform-first cannot work.

One more search worth naming, because it's the honest counter-test: a systematic sweep across five "design-first" communities turned up no Level-2-or-better evidence of a company that redesigned its org for AI first and then saw AI work better. That doesn't mean "never redesign." It refines the thesis: the redesign should be informed by competence, not run ahead of it. (repo counter-evidence search — a null result, reported as one.)

Use when

A vendor is in your calendar before anyone in the building has built an agent — a procurement cycle opening on zero internal competence, leadership "excited about AI," or an isolated experiment that "worked" with nothing connecting it to the next one.

Build

Not a platform pick. A competence base plus a scoped, evidence-backed shortlist of the three real infrastructure questions — produced by people who've built, not watched demos.

Test

Domain experts name the candidates and "people build unprompted."
Not "we signed a platform contract."

Core moves

The sequence, in order

An org disposition — the platform node is deliberately last.
1

Refuse procurement-first

Name the default out loud — before the eval grid gets built.

2

Train one person to build

Start on a coding agent. The cheap meta-platform.

3

Let the pull spread

Competence finds its own high-value processes.

4

Let builders find the walls

Data access · runtime · discoverability. Don't pre-assess.

5

Choose the platform last

Small, scoped, two-way door — against your cases.

competence→discovery→context→platform

The repo's strategic frame, and the order is load-bearing: tools commoditise; the organisational learning rate is the ceiling. Each pass leaves the next decision smaller and more reversible.

Fastest way to feel it: do step one yourself. Spin up a coding agent and have it build you one small thing you'd actually use. Claude Code or Codex · ~$20/mo · no board sign-off · no procurement · ~1 hour, before dinner. The moment the abstraction turns concrete is the whole thesis in miniature — and the next platform demo sounds different.

Why
The principle

Clarity is the ceiling, not capability. The bottleneck is organisational, not technical.

"You cannot design an organisation for a capability nobody in it understands."

Without competence there is no vision — only governance of an abstraction. The chain is plain: competence → mental models → shared vision → connected experiments → organisational learning. Skip the first link and the chain never forms; you get the HBR experimentation trap — hundreds of isolated pilots that never scale. The whole point of training before buying is that the first link is the only one you can't import, brief, or procure.

And the timing argument is just as sharp: nobody should be making non-two-way-door decisions on the agent landscape right now — the space is pre-chasm and every platform is immature. Competence-first defers exactly the expensive, irreversible calls and pulls forward the cheap, reversible ones. The person who's built one agent walks into the procurement meeting with evidence. Everyone else walks in with vendor narratives.

Train before you buy — the platform question shrinks to a two-way door.
How you know it's real

The tell isn't a signed contract — it's behaviour. People build unprompted: nobody was assigned "build an agent for X," the competence itself created the pull. (a Nordic security-software org field observation, March 2026 — practitioner-direct, Level 2: after two modules of training, pretty much everyone started building dashboards, agents, applications.)

The questions get smaller and more specific — from "which platform should we standardise on?" to "where does this app live, and how does my colleague find it?" Vague-and-vendor-shaped giving way to scoped-and-reversible is the signal. And the candidates get named by domain experts, not consultants — who are right more often, because they know the work. The negative test: if the only "competence" in the building is a signed contract and a training plan to follow it, the sequence ran backwards.

Intent
Recipe · business lane · phase: Intent · company layer

WOW before strategy

The principle: competence is the ceiling, not capability — you can't envision what you've never used your own hands to build.

Before the strategy offsite, put your people in a room and let each build one real working thing with AI in an afternoon. The WOW creates demand no deck can — and because competence is the ceiling every later platform, governance and team-scale move is bounded by, this is the Intent-phase company move the rest of the transformation rests on. Strategy is the frame; experience is the fuel. If you must sequence them, fuel first.

Deck → nodding. Hands → spreading. You can't sell a future they've never touched.
The reflex that fails · why this transformation is different

Every past transformation rewarded the deck. This one punishes it.

Digital, agile, cloud — every transformation you've run before was vision-led, and rightly so. A CEO could picture a "digital company" through pure analogy, never having written a line of code, and the picture was close enough to align around. So the reflex is hardwired: kick off with a vision, build the strategy, pick the tools, drive adoption. That order has worked your whole career. The trouble is that agents quietly broke the first link in the chain.

Say the words "an agent that autonomously processes invoices across three systems" to someone who has never run one, and you get a polite nod over an empty space. The gap isn't knowledge a slide could close — it's experience, and no deck bridges it. So the honest diagnosis after most AI kickoffs is the most damning one a leader can write down: they nodded, and nothing changed. The reflex didn't misfire; the reflex was the problem. The fix is to run the same four pieces in reverse — the diagram below puts the two orders side by side.

Process diagram · 01Standard change management runs vision → strategy → tools. For AI, run it backwards — WOW → competence → sees-own-future → acts — on a floor of safety.
Named precondition · cited finding, not a coined law

Safety as the floor under the sequence is well-supported as a direction: people won't risk a first attempt where a failed experiment gets them blamed. The specific numbers come from one funded study — Infosys / MIT Technology Review Insights, Dec 2025 — Infosys-funded research, directional (83% of 500 business leaders say psychological safety measurably affects AI-initiative success; only 39% rate their own org's safety "very high"). Treat the direction as solid; treat the percentages as one survey, not an established norm.

Here's the part that stings a builder-leader most, because it demotes the move you're best at. Standing up and telling people AI matters — the thing every change-management playbook tells you to do — has roughly zero direct effect on whether they adopt it. What moves adoption is a colleague saying, in their own words, how AI changed their Tuesday. Your encouragement isn't worthless; it's just indirect. You don't push the change through the org. You set the conditions under which peers carry it for you. The diagram below draws the two leader-shapes: the single thick arrow that bounces off, and the small forum the change spreads out of.

You don't drive AI adoption. You create the conditions for peers to drive it — and then get out of the thread's way.

Process diagram · 02The thick arrow bounces. The forum spreads. Your direct push is ~0pp; the threads peers run between themselves are what move the org.
The peer-influence numbers · name the source genre

The +8.9pp heavy-use / +10.4pp agents / ~0pp direct-leadership figures are from a Microsoft Research academic study, Mar 2026 — call it "the Microsoft Research study," not "research shows." The perception gap (76% of executives believe staff are enthusiastic; 31% are — leaders 2x off) is HBR / Lovich-BCG + Meier-Columbia, Nov 2025. The mandate-resistance multiplier and the 96%-adopt / 4%-ROI tools-first trap are directional reorderings from the same body of field reporting.

The dose · how much hands-on it actually takes

A demo they watch doesn't take. A thing they build does.

The WOW is not a polished demo on a big screen — watching someone else's magic produces applause, not pull. It's the person's own hands on the keyboard, building one small real thing, hitting the moment where the output is genuinely theirs. And it takes a meaningful dose to get there: below some floor people poke at it once, get a mediocre result, and quietly conclude AI "isn't there yet." Above the floor they tip into regular use. In-person beats remote on every measure, because the WOW needs shared air and a colleague leaning over to say "wait, show me how you did that."

How big is "meaningful"? A useful order-of-magnitude exists, but be careful how you carry it. A BCG consultancy-survey finding (directional, Jun 2025) reports 79% of employees with five-plus hours of hands-on time became regular users, versus 67% below — and that only about a third feel properly trained. Take the shape of that: a real dose, not a lunch-and-learn. Do not turn it into a law that "people need five hours" — your threshold depends on your people and your tools. The Mollick MBA experiment points the same direction by a different route: a compelling single experiment (One Useful Thing, Jan 2026) in which non-engineers built working startup prototypes in four days, and the management skills they already had — delegating, judging output, explaining intent — turned out to be the exact AI skills. One cohort, one instructor, unreplicated; persuasive, not proven.

The five-hour number · directional, not a dose law

BCG, Jun 2025 — vendor / consultancy survey, treat as directional. 79% of employees with 5+ hours hands-on became regular users vs 67% below; in-person beat online; only ~33% said they were properly trained. Useful as an order-of-magnitude — "give it a real dose, in person" — not as a proven universal dose. "People need five hours" is a coronation the data doesn't earn; your number depends on your people and tools.

Then the interesting thing happens, and it's the whole reason to start here. People who've built one working thing stop waiting to be told where AI fits. They go find their own high-value process — the report nobody enjoys, the reconciliation that eats a Thursday — because competence creates pull (this shows up in the field, e.g. a Nordic security-software org, where adoption stopped needing a champion once people had the skill). A person who has built a piece of it can finally imagine their own role redesigned around it, which is the muscle that separates AI high-performers from dabblers. The loop below is the engine: build · tell a peer · peer wants in · joins the next session · builds · tells a peer. Each turn the circle of competent builders widens — and strategy rides on top of it, written second.

Process diagram · 03Compound interest on a WOW. Each pass widens the circle of people who can imagine their own role redesigned — and strategy rides on top, written second.
Use when

You're about to kick off the AI transformation and your instinct is a strategy deck, a roadmap, a platform shortlist — or a skeptic won't move on your slides, or adoption stalled after a tools rollout that nobody actually changed behaviour around.

Build

A WOW session where each person built one real thing — plus a standing peer forum: voluntary, recurring, no mandate. The strategy comes second.

Test

People build unprompted, and a skeptic flips on proof they made with their own hands.
Not merely "96% adopted the tool."

Core moves

Run the sequence forwards

WOW → competence → sees-own-future → acts. Same pieces as the deck — reversed.
1

Open with the WOW

Not a demo they watch — a thing they build by hand, in a few hours.

2

Give a real dose, in person

A meaningful hands-on dose beats a lunch-and-learn. Same room.

3

Practice on real work

Their actual reports, not toy tasks. Competence creates pull.

4

Let peers carry it

Make the forum, not the speech. Peers spread the WOW.

5

Bring strategy second

Now competent people argue platforms from their own hands.

build by hand→tell a peer→peer wants in→joins next session→repeat

The forum is the engine, not the speech: compound interest on a WOW. Each pass widens the circle of people who can imagine their own role redesigned — and the strategy you write later has competent people to run it.

Monday move: cancel the offsite, book a room. Five willing people, real laptops, each builds one small real thing by the end — no slides, no roadmap, no goalposts. A calendar invite · a room · two hours · no budget · no platform contract · no board sign-off. Then ask one question — "what would you build next?" — and write down what they say. That list is your strategy input, and they wrote it, not you.

Test · how you know it ran, not just played

The signal that it took is people building unprompted — after a couple of hands-on sessions they start without being told where to look. A skeptic — the rational professional, not a technophobe — flips when they see role-specific proof they made themselves, never from another deck. And the WOW shows up second-hand: a colleague says, in their own words, how watching a coworker use AI changed their mind. The negative test is the tools-first trap dressed as success — high adoption, no behaviour change (96% adopt, 4% see ROI). If the numbers look great and Tuesday looks identical, you shipped tools, not the WOW.

Why
The principle

Competence is the ceiling, not capability. Strategy without competent people is governance of an abstraction.

"You can't envision what you've never experienced — so stop selling the future and let them build a piece of it."

The deck doesn't land because it can't: the perception gap (76% of executives believe staff are enthusiastic; 31% are) means leaders are reasoning about a room that isn't there. The mechanism underneath is mental-model formation — a person who has built one working thing can finally picture their own role redesigned around AI, and the people who redesign their workflow are the ones who become high performers (a McKinsey consultancy survey, directional, puts them 2.8x more likely). You cannot deck your way to that mental model. You have to hand them the keyboard.

The counter-evidence is real and resolves cleanly. Deloitte (consultancy, directional) finds formal-strategy orgs report far higher implementation success — but strategy and experience are complementary, not competing: strategy is the frame, experience is the fuel. Shopify's AI mandate worked because the CEO already had the WOW in his own hands; the mandates that failed came from leaders who hadn't. So frame, then fuel — and if forced to sequence, fuel first. Note the worst-case path too: a mandate without the experience underneath buys you compliance and roughly 2.2x the resistance.

Frame, then fuel. If forced to sequence — fuel first.
Intent
Pattern · business lane · phase: Intent · the seed the compounding system is grown around

Choose the one live challenge

The principle: persistence plus automation equals system — but a system can only compound around something that recurs.

Before you wrap any agent in sources, memory and a schedule, pick the one live, recurring, high-value challenge worth building around — the choice that decides whether everything downstream compounds or scatters.

Same system, two challenges. The fork is the choice — the soil decides the ceiling.
The mechanism · why the terrain decides the ceiling

The system inherits the quality of the challenge.

Here is the move everyone skips because it looks like it isn't a move at all: before you build the agent, decide what you're building it around. The recipe for a compounding system opens with "pick the live challenge" and then never dwells on it — the selection is assumed, so the reader assumes it too, and aims at whatever's easiest to specify. That's the trap. The machinery — raw sources kept on disk, a memory that compiles them, an agent that runs, a scheduled morning touch — is the same whatever you point it at. What changes is whether the thing you wrapped it around comes back. A folder of markdown can compound; a folder of markdown wrapped around a one-off compounds nothing.

The cleanest way to feel it is to put two candidates through the same machinery. On the left, a task: "draft this memo." It finishes. The loop opens and never returns; the memory has nothing to sharpen against, because nothing ran twice. On the right, a challenge: "keep the programme's commitments from slipping." It recurs — next week, next quarter, whether you built for it or not — so the loop closes back on itself and the memory is a little sharper every pass. Same machinery, opposite outcome. Below is the picture.

Process diagram · 01Same machinery, opposite outcome. A task's loop opens and never returns; a challenge's loop closes back on itself and the memory sharpens each pass.

So how do you tell a challenge from a task wearing a challenge's clothes? Run each candidate through three gates, in series, and be ruthless. Live — is it currently open, a thing you are carrying right now, not a hypothetical someday-problem? Recurring — does the work run again, so a memory has something to sharpen against? High-value — is it worth the build, paid work and not a toy? Most candidates fall out at one gate. A toy fails value; a one-off fails recurrence; a someday-problem fails live. The intersection that clears all three is small on purpose — and that scarcity is the point.

A toy fails value. A one-off fails recurrence. A someday-problem fails live. The intersection is small on purpose.

The selection · three gates in series

Three filters. Most candidates fall out.

The instinct after a chat win is to scale the trick: the agent just drafted your memo beautifully, so the next thought is "automate something like that." But the freshest annoyance is rarely the standing one. The challenge worth a compounding system is usually the thing that's been open in your head for weeks, maybe longer — not the task that happens to be easy to specify this afternoon. The funnel below is what stops you building a beautiful system around the wrong soil.

Process diagram · 02Three gates in series. A toy fails value, a one-off fails recurrence, a someday-problem fails live — the one that clears all three is the chosen challenge.

There's a second trap waiting even once you've chosen well, and it's the most common build mistake of all: reaching straight for automation. The hardest-won reusable lesson from operators who've actually shipped these systems is the opposite of the instinct — build a state memory first; do not start with automation; start with a maintained picture of the work. The schedule is not the prize. The maintained picture is the prize, and the morning automation is just what keeps the picture fresh. Choosing the challenge well means choosing one where a maintained picture would be genuinely useful before any automation runs at all. If the memory alone wouldn't earn its keep, the soil is thin no matter how clever the schedule.

The build order · depth before speed

State first. Automation last.

The picture below draws the build as depth, not speed. First the raw sources get curated into a state memory worth reading on its own — that's the load-bearing layer. Then, and only then, a schedule wraps it. Reverse the order and you get a fast loop emitting output nobody trusts, with no maintained picture underneath to make tomorrow's output better than today's. The arrow that matters runs downward into depth, not rightward into speed.

Process diagram · 03Depth before speed. The maintained picture forms first and earns its keep on its own; the schedule wraps it last, only to keep it fresh.
What "Test" actually means · in practice

The test is whether it's still the right thing to build for after a week.

You know you chose well not on the day you choose, but a week later. The challenge should still be the right thing to be building for — it didn't finish, it didn't go stale, it's still open. The honest negative test is one question: "does this come back next week?" If the only truthful answer is "no, it's done once," you chose a task. Re-choose. A system built around a one-off is the most expensive way ever invented to do something a single time. And there's a positive tell worth trusting: if the maintained picture alone is genuinely useful — if the memory earns its keep before any automation runs — the soil is rich and everything you grow in it will compound.

Use when

You're about to point an agent at something and "what should I automate first?" is the live question — at the start of any build, right after a chat win, or at a quarter boundary when the open challenge has quietly shifted.

Build

A one-sentence seed challenge.md — the live, recurring, high-value challenge — plus a three-line sketch of its sources, its state, and its recurring output.

Test

A week later it's still the right thing to build for.
Not "done once."

Core moves

The action, in sequence

A choice you make in a text editor — no platform, no schedule yet.
1

Surface the standing one

Not the freshest annoyance — the one open in your head for weeks.

2

Reject the task

Does it come back next week regardless? If it finishes, it's a task.

3

Test all three at once

Live · recurring · high-value. Fail one, re-choose.

4

Picture the system

Raw sources? State worth keeping? A recurring output a schedule carries?

5

State first, not automation

Choose where a maintained picture is the prize. The schedule comes last.

surface→reject the task→test all three→picture the system→state first

Get this one right and everything downstream compounds; get it wrong and a beautiful system scatters around nothing. The choice is the precondition the whole build inherits.

The most consequential decision in the build is the one you can make tonight, alone. A blank challenge.md · three honest questions · no connector · no budget · no sign-off · ~15 min. Connectors and scheduling come later, when the system grows around the choice. The choice itself is free and reversible.

Why
The principle

Persistence plus automation equals system — but only around something that recurs.

"A system compounds around the challenge you choose, or it scatters around the one you didn't."

The choice of challenge is the highest-leverage decision in the whole build, and it's the one everyone skips. The recipe opens with "pick the live challenge" and then never dwells on it — so the reader doesn't either, and aims at whatever's easy to specify. But a chat can't compound; a folder of markdown can; and a folder of markdown wrapped around a one-off compounds nothing either. The terrain decides the ceiling.

This is why the very first agent build is deliberately a rehearsal on something trivial — to feel what a compounding system does before you stake it on the work that has to stand up. The work that has to stand up is chosen, not stumbled into. Pick the wrong challenge and you can build a flawless system that accretes nothing; pick the right one and even an ordinary build compounds.

Where it sits: this is the Intent-phase seed of the business lane — the precondition the compounding system assumes but never patterns, and the amber twin of make output yours in the personal lane. Choose well once and you have one maintained picture; choose well across functions and a builder-leader ends up with a portfolio of maintained pictures the whole organisation can stand work on — not a graveyard of one-off agent demos. The choice is what makes the agentic effort accrete at company scale instead of scattering across clever tricks.

The terrain decides the ceiling.
Intent
Recipe · R1 · the first move on any agent file

Make output yours

The principle: Context is King — a cleverer prompt won't save you; structured context will.

Steer the agent with structured context until the output sounds like a real person or company, not the LLM — by changing what the agent sees, not how cleverly you ask.

The agent isn't generic. Your context is — the guardrail is the only thing that changed.
The mechanism · how the sausage is made

Same words, different answer.

The most useful thing to understand about a coding agent is also the most unglamorous: it isn't looking your question up in a database. Every turn, it re-reads the whole conversation and generates the next response from all of it. Your first prompt and its answer are now part of the input to the second prompt. Change the front, change the back. That's it. That's the lever everything else in this operating model — tools, goals, checks, boundaries, loops — sits on top of. None of them work unless the agent reads the right world first.

The cleanest demonstration takes ninety seconds. Open three fresh windows. In each one, ask "What should we have for dinner?" as the second turn — but vary the first. Window A's first turn is "What is the capital of Italy?" / "Rome." Window B's first turn is "What is the largest lake in Finland?" / "Saimaa." Window C's first turn is "I'm a cardiologist preparing dinner for my patients." Same exact follow-up. Three answers that drift Italian, Finnish, and heart-healthy respectively. Below is the picture — the diagram you can run yourself before lunch.

Process diagram · 01Same words. Different answer. The first exchange became context, and the context coloured everything after.

The context that colours output isn't only nationality. It can be a fact, a role, a preference, a constraint — anything you tell the agent. Window C's answer shifts not because Claude suddenly knows medicine better than it knows Italian cooking, but because you told it who you are and every answer after took that into account. The mechanism is dumb and total: whatever you put in front, you'll find pulled through to the back. Garbage in, garbage back. Specifics in, specifics back. The shape of what you give it is the shape of what you get.

A cleverer prompt won't manufacture facts you never gave it. Only structured context can.

The shelf-life upgrade · from chat to file

From the fading message to the file the agent reads cold.

What we just did was an ephemeral message — typed into a chat, gone when the window closes. Powerful per session, useless next Monday. The move that survives the weekend is the same mechanism with a different shelf life: turn that context into a file the agent reads at the start of every conversation. CLAUDE.md in a Claude Code project. A rules file the agent loads cold. Same physics — the agent reads it as part of the input — but now the steering is durable, version-controlled, and starts the next session sharper than the last one ended. Below: chat-bubble fading on the left; rule file glowing on the right.

Process diagram · 02Guardrails are structured context, not a checklist. A file the agent reads cold makes the next session start sharper than the last one ended.

The compounding step is where most teams under-invest, and where the gap with serious operators widens fastest. The first version of any rule file is never exactly right. Two paragraphs are too thin; ten paragraphs are noise the agent skims past. You only find out which two were the load-bearing ones by using the file again, noticing what the agent still got wrong, and editing. Same move you used here on a one-pager, you'll use on every agent file from now on — module 1 lands the muscle; later modules systematise it.

The compounding loop · what changes between passes

The rule file gets sharper every time you put it to work.

The picture below shows the four-beat loop with the file itself getting visibly denser between passes. Notice the order: you do the work first — you don't sit and write rules in the abstract. Reflection without a real run produces opinions, not guardrails. Then you capture what mattered. Then you reflect. Then you sharpen the file. Then you do the next piece of work, which is the first run against the sharper file, which is also the first place you discover what's still missing. Compound interest on a rule file. Boring on day one; dominant by day thirty.

Process diagram · 03Compound interest on a rule file. The first pass is never exactly right; the rule file gets sharper every time you put it to work.
What "Test" actually means · in practice

The test that matters is "yes, that's it."

The test that matters is "yes, that's it" from someone who knows the subject cold — not "that's polished" from a stranger, and not "looks good" from Claude itself. Polish-praise rounds corners. Asked to comment on a stranger's bio you'd reach for "reads well, nice tone." Asked about your own bio, the wrong adjectives jump off the page like a typo. Domain expertise is the eval. When you read the output, push back on anything that doesn't match your own gut; that's the pattern. Every time you do the work and reflect, the rule file gets sharper, and the next pass needs less pushing-back to land. This is also why module 1 of Agents 101 puts you on a one-pager about yourself — you cannot fool yourself on your own material, which is exactly the calibration you need to spot fabrication everywhere else later.

Use when

The agent keeps producing generic prose, pages, pitches, profiles or memos that need to sound like a real person or company — and you catch yourself blaming the model, or hunting for a cleverer prompt.

Build

A first artifact — plus the guardrails that make the next one sharper. A reusable rule file you keep.

Test

Someone who knows the subject says "yes, that's it."
Not merely "that's polished."

Core moves

The action, in sequence

Reusable on any work — not a branding exercise.
1

Generate the thin baseline

Run it cold first. See the grey — that's your before.

2

Name the real audience

Who is this actually for? Tell the agent, specifically.

3

Add the facts only you know

The details no model could guess. This is the steering.

4

Compare versions

Before vs after, side by side. The gap is the lesson.

5

Catch the fabrication

Where you're the expert, spot what it made up.

6

Save the useful rules

Write the guardrails down. Next run starts smarter.

do the work→capture the rules→reflect→sharpen→repeat

Then it's a habit, not a task: compound interest on a rule file. Each pass leaves the next one starting smarter — the move you reuse on every agent file, forever.

Fastest way to feel it: something you know cold. A one-pager about yourself. Vanilla Claude Code · your own LinkedIn · no org data · no platform · no budget · ~45 min. You'll catch every flattened line instantly — this is literally the first hour of Agents 101.

Why
The principle

Context is King. The agent isn't the lever — what it sees is.

"You are the one evaluator you cannot fool on your own content."

The agent isn't generic — your context is. Average output becomes great not because you prompted harder, but because the guardrail is the control. A cleverer prompt cannot manufacture facts you never gave it; only structured context can. That's why the move is structural, not stylistic.

This works because you are the one evaluator you cannot fool on your own material. Asked to comment on a stranger's bio, you'd reach for "looks polished." Asked about your own, the wrong adjectives jump off the page. Spotting fabrication on something you know cold is the foundation skill everything later in the operating model — verification, evals, judges, autonomy — is built on. Skip this and the rest is theatre.

The agent isn't generic. Your context is.
Intent
Recipe · software · phase: Intent · the first move of every session

Read the room before you run

The principle: Context is King — and an unexamined window quietly biases every move after it.

Before you paste the task, make the agent's read of the repo an inspected fact, not a fluent assumption: ask for a deliberate read, interrogate what it skipped, quote one file back, and check the budget you have left. A checked read is the precondition for evidence worth compounding into the shared kit — the whole org's learning loop inherits the quality of its orientation habit.

The summary sounded oriented. Orientation is what you checked — the skip list, one quote-back, and the budget.
The mechanism · why fluency fools you

The agent's confidence tracks its prose, not its accuracy.

Here is the trap, and it is a good one. When you open a session and ask the agent to look at the repo, it reports back fluently, specifically, reassuringly — and it does this whether or not it read the right files. The prose is calibrated; the read may not be. That is the design, not a bug: you prime it, the LLM scales whatever you primed. A vague prime — "have a look at the repo" — gets scaled into a vague, shallow, partly-reconstructed read, delivered with the same poise as a careful one. Fluency is not evidence. The cost of mistaking one for the other doesn't show up now; it shows up three steps later as a fix aimed at the wrong file.

The fork is the prime, and the diagram below draws it. Send the agent in vague and it scales your vagueness: it names what it happened to glance at and stops. Send it in deliberate — "read what's load-bearing, skip what isn't worth it, then tell me what you skipped and why" — and you get an inspected read with its own seams showing. Same repo, same model, two completely different substrates for everything downstream. The whole operating model rides on whichever one you produced in the first five minutes.

Process diagram · 01Same repo, same model. The prime is the fork — a vague look scales to a shallow read; a deliberate one scales to an inspected read with its own skip list showing.

The deliberate prime gets you a better read — but a better read is still a claim, not ground truth. The agent's account of what it read and why is a reconstruction, and reconstructions confabulate: it will sometimes give you a tidy reason for a file it never actually opened. So the second move is to stop nodding and start interrogating. Ask the one question almost nobody asks — "what did you skip, and why?" The skip list is where the risk lives, and the agent rarely volunteers it. Then spot-check: quote one specific file or function back and ask what's actually in it. Claims aren't evidence until you've checked one.

The agent's self-report is a hypothesis, not ground truth. Treat it like one.

The upgrade · from summary you nod at to read you checked

Turn the read from a one-way summary into a checked artefact.

The upgrade is cheap and it changes the epistemics entirely. A one-way summary asks for your trust; a checked read earns it. You surface the read-vs-skipped split, you quote-check one claim against the actual file, and you run /context to see the budget — the number and the breakdown across system prompt, messages, memory and skills. The slice the agent didn't load is the bounded-window reality you're now steering inside. Below: the summary on the left that you'd otherwise nod at, and the same read on the right after the arrow tagged "fluency → evidence."

Process diagram · 02Fluency → evidence. The read becomes a checked artefact — skip list surfaced, one claim quote-checked, the budget read. Assume a working ~10% of what the agent says is misrepresentation until you've checked one — a curriculum heuristic, could be more or less; the point is to check, not to trust the number.
Working heuristic

The "~10% misrepresentation" figure is a curriculum-stated working assumption, not a measured rate — could be more, could be less. Its job is to make you spot-check one claim, not to be reasoned from as if it were a finding. Wherever the number appears on this page, that caveat travels with it.

Orientation isn't a one-shot ritual you perform at session start and forget. It's a loop, and it tightens. Each pass you orient, you ask what got skipped, you quote-check a claim, you read /context — and then you spend the next round's bytes more deliberately because you now know which ones were wasted last time. The unread slice shrinks toward the part that genuinely doesn't matter. The session that produces a clean, checked read is also the one whose evidence the downstream compound step can actually trust and encode. Garbage orientation in, garbage to compound from. A checked read out, something worth keeping.

The compounding loop · what changes between passes

Each pass, the unread slice shrinks toward what doesn't matter.

The picture below draws the four beats with the window's unread wedge getting visibly thinner across passes. Notice it never closes to zero — orientation isn't about reading everything, which would just burn the budget you came to protect. It's about driving the unread slice down to the part you've consciously decided is safe to leave out. That conscious leaving-out is the skill. By the third pass you're not reading more; you're reading righter, and you can say exactly what's not in the window and why that's fine.

Process diagram · 03The unread slice shrinks, but never to zero. Each pass you read righter, not more — and you can say exactly what's not in the window and why that's fine.
What "Test" actually means · in practice

You're not testing the summary. You're testing whether you checked.

The honest test is uncomfortable, because it indicts the most natural thing to do. If you read the agent's summary, nodded, and moved straight to the fix — you skipped the move, however oriented the summary sounded. So the test is falsifiable and it lives in the scrollback: can you name one file the agent chose not to read, and say whether that matches what you'd have expected? Did you quote one file back and watch the claim hold — or catch it where it didn't? Can you point at the /context percentage and say which slice of the repo is not in the window right now? Three yeses and you oriented. Any no and you're steering blind in fluent prose. That last one — catching the fluent-but-wrong — is the foundation skill everything downstream leans on: the plan you'll pressure-test, the test you'll write first, the evidence you'll compound. Skip orientation and all of it inherits an unchecked map.

Use when

You're about to set an agent loose in a repo and you haven't checked what it can actually see — every session start, every switch of repo or feature, and every time a session goes sideways and you realise it was working from a map you never checked.

Build

A checked orientation — not a document you keep, a state you reach: the read, its read-vs-skipped account, one confirmed quote-back, and a /context reading. The map is inspected, not assumed.

Test

You can name one file it didn't read, one claim you quote-checked, and the unread slice.
Not merely "the summary read well."

Core moves

The action, in sequence

Three messages and one slash command — before any code moves.
1

Ask for a deliberate read

Shape, load-bearing, stale — and skip what isn't worth it. Recruit its judgment, not completeness.

2

Interrogate the skip list

"What did you skip, and why?" The risk hides where it didn't look.

3

Quote one file back

"You said you read X — what's in it?" Treat the report as a hypothesis.

4

Read the budget left

Run /context. The unread slice is the reality you steer inside.

orient→introspect→spot-check→read /context→steer the next bytes

Then it's a reflex, not a ritual: the unread slice shrinks every pass. The same first move you make before every session, on every repo, forever — and the precondition for every checked artefact downstream.

Monday move: before you paste the task, slow down for five minutes. Ask for a deliberate read, then "what did you skip, and why?", quote one file back, run /context, look at the number. A repo you already have open · /context is built in · no platform · no budget · no sign-off · before a line of code moves. It costs only the reflex to slow down now instead of paying for it three steps later.

Why
The principle

Context is King. You prime, the LLM scales — including your vagueness.

"The agent's self-report is a hypothesis, not ground truth."

The counterintuitive part is that the agent's confidence is calibrated to its prose, not its accuracy. It flatters, it progresses, it mirrors your stance — reporting the repo fluently whether or not it read the right files. Two mechanisms ride underneath. First, context is whatever you tell it: the window colours everything downstream, so an unexamined window quietly biases every later move — the wrong feature read becomes the wrong fix, three steps on. Second, the window has a ceiling: every byte spent on noise is a byte not available for the work, so seeing the budget is what lets you spend it on purpose.

Orientation is how you make the prime deliberate — and how you check the right context actually loaded. Skipping it doesn't save time; it moves the cost downstream, where it's more expensive to find. A checked read is the substrate the plan, the failing test, and the compounded evidence all ride on. Skip this and the rest is built on a map you never looked at.

You can't steer what you can't see.
Test · the negative case

The fastest tell you skipped the move: the scrollback shows no /context in the first ten minutes, no introspection prompt after the read, and no quote-back when something felt off. A clean orientation leaves all three as deliberate moves in the transcript — "you said you read X, what's in it?" lands before the first edit, not after the wrong one.

Intent
Recipe · software · Intent → Context · a recognition move

Name the three blocks

The principle: recognition before naming — a frame is only trustworthy once you've watched it fit your own mess.

Sort the context you already keep — rules, decisions, quality bars — into three named kinds, and let the slot that comes up empty tell you what the agent is missing. You're not authoring; you're auditing a pile you already built.

The lines didn't change. The empty lane did — and an empty lane is what the agent never inherited.
The mechanism · why a sort changes nothing and reveals everything

The lines don't change. The slots do.

You have a CLAUDE.md, probably a CLAUDE.local.md, a few observations jotted down, an ADR or two, a skill you wrote last week. Each was written in the moment, for its own reason, and nobody ever stepped back to ask what kind of thing each one is. So when a real task lands and you go to walk your material against it, you're reading a flat list with no shape — and a flat list is exactly the surface that hides its own holes. Presence is easy to see; absence is invisible. You can stare at twenty good lines and feel well-prepared, because the missing twenty-first leaves no mark on the page.

The move is borrowed, and it travels with its source attached: Huryn's three-block memory — a frame for naming what you've built, not a template to fill in. Sort every line of context into one of three kinds. Block 1 is observation → rule: the conditioned reflexes you've encoded — we use Postgres, not Mongo; webhook signatures get validated before dispatch. Block 2 is decisions plus the alternatives you rejected — the choice, the road not taken, the constraint that forced it. Block 3 is quality criteria — what "done" looks like, what you'd reject the output for. Same lines, three labelled slots. Below: the identical pile, before and after the sort.

Process diagram · 01The lines didn't change — the slots did, and an empty slot is a finding. Not new content; new legibility.

Here's the counterintuitive part, and it's the whole reason the move is worth five minutes: the value isn't in the rules you've written — it's in the category that's empty. A sort doesn't add a single line. What it adds is a structure with named slots, so that one slot sitting bare becomes impossible to un-see. That's the cognitive trick the frame plays — it converts an absence (no quality criteria) into a presence (an empty Block 3 staring back at you). The bare lane is louder than every full one. You can argue with a rule; you can't argue with a slot that has nothing in it.

A flat list flatters the pile. The empty block tells you the truth.

Two slots tend to come up short, and each absence costs the agent something specific. A thin Block 2 means decisions were made and then forgotten — the agent inherits the what but not the why, so it cheerfully proposes the alternative you already rejected for a reason it never learned. A decision recorded with no rejected alternative is itself a finding: a Block 2 entry missing half its content. And Block 3 is, in practice, the emptiest of the three — not because it's a measured rate, but because most engineers carry their quality bar in their head and never wrote it down, so the agent never inherits the taste that would let it reject its own bad output. The sort doesn't fix this. It just makes the hole stop hiding.

The upgrade move · template-filled → recognition-audited

Point the lens at your own mess, never a blank template.

There are two ways to arrive at a three-block memory, and only one survives contact with a task. The tempting path starts from a blank template: open three empty headings and dutifully author rules until each block looks full. It produces a tidy, complete-looking system that was never tested against real work — context that reads well and means nothing, because you wrote what you imagined your standards were, not what your repo has actually been enforcing. The honest path runs backwards: point the frame at the material you already wrote and classify what's there. Recognition, not authoring. The frame earns its name after you've matched a real line to a block — never before. Below: both paths, and the one that holds.

Process diagram · 02Authoring from a blank template yields tidy context never tested against work. Recognising the blocks in lived material yields an honest audit — gaps and all.

The frame is permanent; the contents compound. The first sort is a snapshot — it tells you which kind of context is load-bearing today and which is missing. But the real return comes from running the loop: a task lands, you sort, the thinnest block surfaces, you fill the worst gap by routing it to its proper home, you send the work off, and the return sharpens the blocks for the next pass. The three lanes are fixed; the lines inside them grow. Each lap the bare lane carries one more line, and the next task starts against a richer map than the last. Boring on the first lap; decisive by the tenth.

Process diagram · 03The frame is permanent; the contents compound. Each lap the bare lane carries one more line, and the next task starts against a richer map.
What "Test" actually means · in practice

The frame has to fit your own ADR — not a textbook example.

The sort worked if you can point at any line in your context and say which block it is without hesitating. A line that resists classification isn't a mystery third category — it's either redundant, or it's quietly doing two jobs and should be split. The harder test is the honest one: at least one block should come up thin or empty, and you should be able to name what that absence costs the agent on the very next task. A sort where all three lanes look full means one of two things — you have unusually mature context, or you're flattering the pile. When in doubt, re-check Block 3; it's the easiest to fool yourself about. And the negative test that catches the most common failure: if you could only illustrate the blocks with invented examples and not one line of your own, the sort hasn't happened. You've learned a vocabulary, not audited a system. The proof is recognising your last real ADR as a Block 2 entry, not nodding along to a clean definition.

Use when

You've accumulated rules, memory, ADRs and skills and you can't tell whether you've built a system or a heap — typically right before you send a real slice off to an agent and want to know the context is load-bearing.

Build

Not a new file — an index over the files you already keep: each line tagged Block 1 / 2 / 3, with the thin or empty block named as a gap to fill before send-off.

Test

The frame fit your own material.
Not a textbook example.

The action, in sequence

Recognition, not authoring — five minutes, no new writing until the end.
1

Point the lens at real material

Open your actual files. Never a blank template.

2

Sort into Block 1

Observation → rule. The encoded reflexes.

3

Sort into Block 2

Decisions + the alternatives you rejected.

4

Sort into Block 3

Quality criteria. What "done" looks like.

5

Read the empty block

The bare lane names the gap for you.

sort→read the empty block→fill the worst gap→send off→return sharpens→repeat

The frame is permanent; the contents compound. Each lap the bare lane carries one more line — the same lens that audits your files will, later, read a team's and a company's.

Monday move: before your next real send-off, open CLAUDE.md and CLAUDE.local.md side by side. Tag each line 1, 2 or 3. Notice which block is empty. Write one line in it before you dispatch. Vanilla Claude Code · your own files · no platform · no budget · no sign-off · ~5 min. This is the recognition move from the first experiment in Agentic Engineering 101 — the sort that turns a pile into an audited system.

Why
The principle

Recognition before naming. A frame is only worth trusting once you've watched it fit your own mess.

"The empty block is the one telling you the truth."

A flat list of rules hides its own holes; a list sorted by kind makes the holes shout. The value isn't in the rules you've written — it's in the category that's empty. That's the cognitive trick the frame plays: it converts an absence (no quality criteria) into a presence (an empty Block 3 staring back at you). Authoring from a blank template produces tidy context that was never tested against a real task; recognising the blocks in lived material produces an honest audit, gaps and all.

Carried correctly, the move travels with its source: Huryn's three-block memory — a frame for naming what you've built, not a template to fill in. And the claim that the value lives in the empty block is a teaching frame, not a measured law — there's no "empty blocks cause N% of failures." It's a lens for seeing absence, and that's exactly enough: you can only trust a structure you've seen fit your own pile.

Presence is easy to see. Absence is the finding.
Intent
Recipe · software · phase: Intent · the move that makes a long run possible

Name the done before you dispatch

The principle: a task is only as dispatchable as its done is checkable — the bottleneck isn't the agent's stamina, it's your willingness to commit a finish line.

Before you send an agent off to run for hours, state a done you can check in one sentence, then decide out loud whether this is a send-off (a checkable finish, packaged enough to run on its own) or a nudge (step-by-step work you'll babysit). The sentence is the deliverable — not the dispatch.

Same task, same agent. The only changed variable is whether a checkable done was named first.
The mechanism · why a long run runs at all

The bottleneck isn't the agent. It's the sentence you skipped.

Here's the unglamorous truth about long-running agent work: the thing that decides whether the next four hours happen with you or without you is not the agent's stamina. It's whether you committed to a finish line before you pressed send. You point a capable agent at a migration, a gnarly refactor, a test-coverage push — and twenty minutes in you're answering questions, correcting paths, re-explaining the goal. You've become the agent. The diagnosis is almost never that the model ran out of road. It's that you dispatched something you never gave a checkable done, so it had nothing of its own to steer toward and you had nothing to check it against.

Watch the same task split in two depending on one variable. Send "modernise the auth module" and the agent has no destination — so it asks, and you narrate, and the whole value of an async tool collapses back into synchronous babysitting. Send "auth reads its config from the new provider, the existing suite stays green" and there's a target the agent points at and a thing you can check on return — without re-reading every line it wrote. Same backlog item. Same agent. The difference is one sentence, written before the dispatch, not after.

Process diagram · 01Same task, two outcomes. The named done is the hinge between work that needs you and work that doesn't.

We resist naming the done because naming it feels like premature commitment — what if the shape changes mid-run? So we dispatch vague intent and tell ourselves we'll "stay close to steer." That instinct is exactly backwards. The done isn't a contract you must hit first try; it's a steering target — the thing the agent points at and the thing you check the trace against. Stay-close-to-steer is how a four-hour async capability quietly becomes a four-hour synchronous chore. Commit the finish line to a sentence and the run gets to happen without you narrating each step.

A vague intent doesn't make the agent dumber. It removes the only thing it could have aimed at.

The deliberate cut · send-off or nudge

Decide the mode out loud — send-off, or nudge.

Naming the done buys you a second, sharper move: the send-off / nudge cut. A send-off has a checkable done and enough context to run on its own; a nudge is step-by-step work you'll deliberately sit in for. Both are legitimate — some work genuinely wants your hand on it. The trap is dispatching a nudge as if it were a send-off, then feeling betrayed when it needs babysitting. That's where the resentment comes from. Naming the mode up front sets your own expectation, so a hands-on run feels like a choice rather than a failure.

The cut has a second axis: size. Reject the typo-fix — the agent crunches it in one shot and you learn nothing about its reach. Reject the quarter-long epic — it won't cohere over a long crunch window, and you'll spend the whole run re-anchoring it. Aim for the slice in between: a real piece of work that genuinely needs sustained coherence, requirement-weaving, and multi-file reasoning — the properties that make something a long-running task rather than a one-shot. Below: the sizing dial, crossed by the checkable-done axis that routes the task to step away or sit in.

Process diagram · 02Size picks the slice; the checkable done picks the mode. Naming both up front is the cut — and it's a decision, not a discovery you make twenty minutes in.

One reframe unlocks the willingness to dispatch at all: every send-off is an experiment, not a production run you need to get right the first time. The done is the steering target you point the experiment at — not a deliverable you're contractually bound to. Stopping a run when you've seen enough is reading, not failing. That distinction is what lets you press send instead of polishing the prompt forever, waiting for a certainty that never arrives. The first done you write will be the hardest one you ever write, precisely because you're treating it as a contract when it's only a target.

The compounding loop · the next done gets easier

Each dispatch teaches you what a nameable done feels like.

The loop below closes the way good habits do: name the done · dispatch · read the trace against it · the next done gets easier to name. Every dispatched task teaches you what a checkable finish line feels like on your own codebase — which slices cohere over a long window, which dissolve into questions, what a stranger needs in the sentence to check it. Your scoping sharpens run over run. The teams that under-invest here keep re-learning the first lesson on every task; the operators who treat the done as a reusable skill compound it. Boring on day one; a different relationship with your backlog by day thirty.

Process diagram · 03The first done is the hardest you'll ever write. Each dispatch teaches you what a nameable done feels like on your codebase — so your scoping sharpens run over run.
What "Test" actually means · in practice

The done is named when a stranger can check it.

The test for a named done is not "sounds clear to me" — you wrote it; of course it does. It's the read-back test: hand the one sentence to someone who hasn't seen the task and ask them to state what "finished" looks like. If they come back with "finished by what measure?", the done isn't named yet — it's still living in your head, not in the sentence. The harder test arrives on return: when the run reports back, can you check it against the done, or only against the agent's own summary? If the only evidence you have is the model's cheerful "shipped most of it, hit a snag on X," you named a vibe, not a done. RLHF-trained models will frame partial failures as partial successes — so a real done has to be checkable independent of the agent's self-report. And the live tell: if you catch yourself re-explaining the goal mid-run, the done was never named. That's the negative test, and it fires whether you wanted it to or not.

Use when

You've got an agent that could run for hours unattended, and a backlog you keep meaning to hand it — but every attempt turns into you typing every step. The async capability has outrun your scoping habit.

Build

A one-sentence done written where the dispatch and your future self can both read it, an explicit send-off-or-nudge call, and a sized slice — neither typo nor epic.

Test

A stranger reads the sentence and says "that's what finished looks like."
Not merely "sounds clear to me."

Core moves

The action, in sequence

A scoping habit you reuse on every backlog item — not a one-off ritual.
1

Name the done in one sentence

State the finish line a stranger could check. Can't say it? It's a wish.

2

Cut send-off from nudge

Decide the mode out loud. Step away, or sit in — not both by accident.

3

Size against both failures

Reject the typo. Reject the epic. Aim for the coherent slice.

4

Frame it as an experiment

The done is a target, not a contract. Dispatch to learn.

name the done→dispatch→read the trace→next done is easier

Then it's a habit, not a chore: scoping that sharpens run over run. Each dispatched task teaches you what a nameable done feels like on your own codebase — the first one is the hardest you'll ever write.

Monday move: open your backlog. Find one item you've thought "an agent could probably take the first pass" and have been quietly not handing over. Write its done in one sentence a teammate could check, then make the cut out loud — send-off or nudge? Your own backlog · no platform · no budget · no sign-off · the sentence is the deliverable, not the dispatch. Software engineers do exactly this in the first long-running send-off of Agents 101.

Why
The principle

A task is only as dispatchable as its done is checkable.

"An agent can run for hours unattended. Whether it does depends on one sentence you write before you start."

The counterintuitive bit: the bottleneck on long-running agent work is not the agent's capability — it's your willingness to commit to a finish line before you begin. We dodge naming the done because it feels like premature commitment, and that dodge quietly collapses an async agent back into synchronous babysitting. Reframe the done as a steering target, not a contract, and the resistance dissolves: you're not promising an outcome, you're giving the run something to aim at and yourself something to check it against.

The send-off-vs-nudge cut is the same insight stated as a decision: some work wants your hand on it; the skill is knowing which, and refusing to babysit the work that didn't. Naming the done is the cheapest possible move — one sentence — and it's the one that determines whether the next four hours run with you or without you. Everything downstream assumes it: you can't walk a system against a task you can't state, and you can't package a run whose finish you can't check.

Where it sits: at the personal layer this is a scoping habit. At the team layer a one-sentence done is the unit a teammate can pick up, check, or hand back without re-deriving intent. At the company layer the named done becomes the interface between human intent and unattended agent runs — how an organisation turns a backlog into dispatchable work. An org's ability to run agents unattended is gated on whether its work is routinely scoped to a checkable done; this card is the precondition the rest of the Intent → Context → Work chain rests on.

The agent has the stamina. The sentence is what's missing.
Context & Guardrails
Context & Guardrails
Recipe · R2 · the cookbook spine · appears in 12 of 20 Index dishes

Build a compounding system

The principle: Persistence + automation = system. A chat cannot compound; a folder of markdown can.

Turn a standing challenge into a three-layer folder — raw sources, cite-backed memory, a narrow agent — so each session starts smarter than the one before, without you rebuilding context from scratch.

Same challenge. The chat forgets; the system remembers — and gets sharper.
The mechanism · why context disappears

The bottleneck isn't thinking. It's context that vanishes overnight.

Most CTOs have a standing challenge that never fully resolves — a platform migration, a talent gap, a market position question they keep returning to. Every week they re-open the same browser tabs, reconstruct the same context, re-read the same threads. The thinking isn't the bottleneck. The context is. And every chat window, by design, takes it with it when it closes.

The distinction that matters: if the next session starts from the same place the last one started, that's a chat. Useful in the moment, flat over time. A system is when the next session begins where today's ended — richer, sharper, already knowing what the previous pass established. That difference is not clever prompting. It's two ingredients: persistence and automation. Neither alone is enough.

"A chat cannot compound; a folder of markdown can."

Process diagram · 01The three strata every compounding system needs. Layer confusion doesn't announce itself — it wears a bug as a disguise. In our own runner the in-repo memory convention and Claude Code's home-scoped auto-memory looked identical on disk; agents kept conflating the two, and that one confusion was the common cause of three separate breakages — earlier runs had just masked it with stale state. One agent stalled on the ambiguity and hung the full 1800-second turn cap. Memory mixed with sources, rules mixed with memory — keep the strata separate and the architecture does the work.
The cite-back rule · what prevents smooth hallucination

Memory without cite-back compiles confidently and quietly invents.

The most insidious failure mode in any compounding system isn't obvious nonsense — it's a memory file that reads fluently, makes reasonable claims, and has no way to be checked. Agents smoothly hallucinate each other's memory. The cite-back rule closes that door: every claim in the memory layer carries the source file or URL it came from. When you push back on a claim, there's something to push back at. Without it, you're arguing with a confident mirror.

The rules layer has a different job: it keeps the system's shape consistent between sessions and between agents. Think of it as the standing brief — voice, what counts as a miss, patterns worth banning. It's short on purpose. A narrow rules file is load-bearing; a long one is noise the agent skims past. The PM agent's rules were narrow — a handful of lines. The narrowness was the feature. Build narrow, test with real work, sharpen as misses accumulate.

Process diagram · 02The upgrade isn't a bigger prompt. It's the folder structure — memory layer that persists, cite-back that keeps it honest, rules file that cold-reads on every session start.
The compounding loop · where the system sharpens

Every miss is context you haven't written yet.

You spot mistakes by running the system and watching where it bends — not by reasoning about what the rules should say before you've seen the output. The compounding loop fires after a real run: the agent produces output, you find the miss, you write the rule, and the next pass starts with that miss closed. The durable artifact is never the morning output. It's the memory plus rules that made the next morning better.

The practical implication: treat the first build as a hypothesis, not a finished product. Three folders, one source, one memory file, one narrow agent — that's enough to start a loop. The system's value is not any single output. It's the memory that makes tomorrow's session start where today's ended. Boring on day one; dominant by day thirty — compound interest on a markdown folder.

Process diagram · 03You spot mistakes by running the system and watching where it bends. Each miss becomes a rule. The memory richer; the rules sharper; the next pass starting further ahead.
What "Test" actually means · after a week

The memory is still worth reading after a week — and sharper than day one.

The test line for this pattern has a time component, and that's deliberate. A system that produces beautiful output on the first morning and degrades into noise by Friday isn't compounding — it's just a very good cold start. Run the system for a week, come back to the memory file, and ask whether you'd actually read it. If the answer is yes, and if you can trace every material claim to a source, the system is working. If the memory has grown fluffy, the cite-back rule wasn't enforced. If you wouldn't read it, the memory layer is summarising rather than maintaining.

The negative test is a general failure mode, not a war story: skip cite-back and a memory file quietly swells with unsourced "context" — and when you later ask the agent to trace a claim, it will confidently invent a source rather than admit it can't. A polished daily output hides it; the rot is in the layer underneath. The durable artifact wasn't the morning output. It was the memory plus rules that made the next morning better — and those had been neglected. Cite-back isn't bureaucracy. It's the mechanism by which the system stays honest under repetition.

Use when

The work should persist, sharpen, and run again without you rebuilding context every time. The challenge is live, stakes are real, and recurrence is guaranteed — it will come up again before Friday. If the next session starts from the same place the last one started, that's a chat, not a system.

Build

Three folders and a root rules file: sources/ · memory/ · agents/ · CLAUDE.md. A house-style file. A scheduled recurring output. The system, running.

Test

The system is still worth reading after a week, and the memory is sharper than the day it started.
Not merely a good first morning output.

Core moves

The action, in sequence

What changes = the system's ability to remember and sharpen.
1

Name the live challenge

One file — challenge.md. A specific, unsolved thing you're actually paid to move. Not "improve our platform." The thing that's been open for weeks.

2

Keep sources raw

Drop originals into sources/ untouched. Resist the urge to summarise pre-ingestion — that's the agent's job.

3

Compile memory with cite-back

The agent writes memory/ — every claim points to the source file or URL it came from. No citation, no claim.

4

Create one narrow agent

One markdown file in agents/. A handful of narrow rules beats a long file. Narrowness is the feature, not the shortcut.

5

Schedule the recurring output

Add fresh evidence, let the memory audit itself, schedule the output. A scheduled touch makes the difference between a build and a system.

challenge surfaces→sources raw→memory compiled→agent runs→miss spotted→rule tightened→repeat

The durable artifact is not the morning output. It's the memory plus rules that made the next morning better. Compound interest on a markdown folder.

Monday move: Open the challenge you've been carrying for two weeks. Create three folders: sources/ memory/ agents/. Drop one source in — a wiki page, a transcript, anything. Ask Claude to write a one-page memory from it, with cite-back. That's the foundation. No platform budget · no team sign-off · no infrastructure. Three folders and one markdown file. You can have a working system before lunch.

Why
The principle

Persistence + automation = system. Neither alone is enough.

"A chat cannot compound; a folder of markdown can."

The bottleneck on your most important challenge is never more thinking. It's context that disappears overnight. A chat gives you the thinking but not the persistence. A folder gives you the persistence. Automation — a scheduled agent, a recurring output — is what turns a folder into a flywheel. Persistence without automation is just a well-organised archive. Automation without persistence is just a clever one-shot. Combined, each session starts where the last one ended.

The counterintuitive part: the architecture is embarrassingly simple. Three folders. Markdown. A rules file the agent reads cold. That simplicity is load-bearing, not a limitation. The moment you add a vector database, a pipeline, or a managed RAG layer before you've done a single compounding week with plain text, you've optimised the plumbing before you know what you're piping. Start with folders. Graduate to infrastructure when the plain-text system is worth protecting.

Where this sits: This is the personal foundation the entire personal OS rests on — without a compounding memory on your most important challenge, every other pattern in the language (judge loops, team sharing, system-building) is building on sand. Once it exists, it becomes the composable base that make-output-yours feeds voice into, that benchmark-the-judge runs quality checks against, and that the team promotes from personal to shared.
The bottleneck isn't thinking. It's context that vanishes overnight.
Context & Guardrails
Recipe · business lane · Context & Guardrails · personal → company

Scope an agent your org can trust

The principle: You can't tell if your agent is safe by looking at its output. The failure modes don't live where you can read them.

Make an agent safe to point at real systems by naming its residual risk — running the check yourself, not waiting for a clean bill of health that, for a non-deterministic system, will never arrive.

The agent isn't trusted because it looks fine. It's trusted because its boundary, and its one named residual, are on record.
The mechanism · why the output can't tell you

The failure isn't in the output. It's in what you can't see.

Here's the uncomfortable part of pointing an agent at anything real: the demo is no evidence. The agent reads an inbox, a CRM, a repo, and it answers beautifully. The pull is to wire it to act — route the thread, update the ticket, send the draft. But the failure modes that matter are not in the answer you can read. They live in what an attacker buried inside a retrieved email, in what the agent quietly decided to do with a tool, in what a borrowed skill carried in. You can re-read the output a hundred times and never meet them. That is why the CTO instinct — "wait for the security review to come back clean" — never fires: for a non-deterministic system, the clean report does not exist to wait for.
