So the check carries two lenses, not one. A policy lens asks what your org has already decided is off-limits — the data-usage, security and AI-use rules you point the agent at as source material. An agent-risk lens asks the question classical perimeter security never thought to: is this input trying to steer or leak the agent? The two see different things, and the gap between them is the whole point. The diagram below shows one message entering, splitting through both lenses, and landing on a verdict gate — with a third exit the binary classifier never had.

Process diagram · 01Two lenses, one check you authored, three verdicts. The third row — "I can't tell" — is the find, not the gap; it catches the ambiguity a binary classifier would have buried.

Name the agent-risk patterns against your agent — and there's a closed set the source teaches as the working vocabulary: prompt injection direct (planted in the user's own input), prompt injection indirect (planted in a source the agent retrieves and reads), secrets-in-context, tool-confusion, and skill supply-chain. Both injection classes turn well-formed English into the attack surface — which is exactly why the firewall shrugs. The attack is not malformed; it reads like a perfectly polite sentence. Walk each pattern against the specific agent and you stop reasoning about agents in general.

Closed set · vocabulary

These five risk patterns — and the five mitigations below — are the named sets from the source's R4 check: a working vocabulary, not an exhaustive taxonomy of every possible agent attack or defence. Name them faithfully and completely; don't treat either list as the whole universe.

Now the move most teams skip: give every rule three rows, not two. Compliant, violating, and "I can't tell." A binary classifier forces the ambiguous cases into false confidence — it has to pick a side, so it picks wrong with a straight face. The third row catches them and hands them back with the ambiguity intact, named, and addressable. Most rows, run honestly, land on the third. That's not the check failing. That is the first honest map of the surface — and "I can't tell" is a valid, useful output for an agent to produce.

A binary verdict is a confident lie about an ambiguous input. The third row is where the work actually lives.

The upgrade · five mitigations narrow the surface

Risk gets smaller and named — never zero.

Once a risk is named, you clip it. Pick from the closed set of five mitigations: scope (narrow what it can reach), split (separate the agent that reads from the one that acts), filter (strip the poison before it enters context), gate (plan-mode review — the agent proposes, you approve, only then it executes), and review (a second pass before the action lands). Each clips one edge of the blast radius. Crucially, these sit on top of your existing controls — network, IAM, logging, supplier review — they never replace them. Loop design is additive. A leader who concludes "the agent check replaces security" ships a breach.

Process diagram · 02Five named mitigations each clip one edge of the surface, layered above the controls you already run — never instead of them. Risk shrinks and gets named; it never reaches zero.
The compounding loop · what survives the session

The residual you name today is the starting line tomorrow.

After the mitigation, something is still true. Write it down — on record, owned, dated. The report must not pretend a narrower instruction erased the risk; it shows what changed and what stayed. Then comes the move that turns a one-time audit into a standing boundary: compound the operating rule back into the project's CLAUDE.md — what this agent's failure modes are, what to check before it touches the system. The next session reads it on cold start and begins at a stricter line. The loop closes through the rules file in the soil; each pass, the starting line is stricter and the residual list is shorter and more honest.

Process diagram · 03Compound interest on a boundary. The loop closes through CLAUDE.md — each pass the starting line is stricter and the residual list shorter and more honest.
Use when

The agent is about to touch real systems, real data, or a decision someone else relies on — and "the output looks fine" is the only check you have. Recurs at every new connector, action class, data zone, or team inheriting the deployment.

Build

A reusable security check as a personal skill (both lenses, travelling); a report with residuals (three verdicts per rule + the risk you accepted, the one you mitigated, what changed); and operating rules in CLAUDE.md future sessions load first.

Test

The report contains at least one residual you cannot flatten.
Not a clean sheet of all compliant.

Core moves

The action, in sequence

Two lenses, one check you authored, three verdicts. You didn't become a security specialist — you knew what mattered and dictated it.
1

Run the policy files raw

Point it at your policies, once. See the baseline the reusable check must beat.

2

Name the five risk patterns

Direct · indirect injection · secrets · tool-confusion · supply-chain. Walk each against your agent.

3

Give every rule three rows

Compliant · violating · "I can't tell." Most rows land on the third.

4

Mitigate one

Scope · split · filter · gate · review. On top of existing controls, never instead.

5

Name what remains

The residual, owned and dated. Then compound the rule into CLAUDE.md.

run the check→surface the residual→mitigate one→name what remains→compound

Then it's a standing boundary, not a one-time audit: compound interest on a residual list. The next agent you build starts at a stricter line because of this one.

Monday move: pick one agent you already use that touches real data. Open a file · three columns: rule · verdict · evidence · run the five risk patterns · write compliant / violating / "I can't tell." You'll land on "I can't tell" more than you expect — that's the first honest map. Pick the residual that bothers you most, write one sentence naming it. No platform, no budget, no sign-off.

Test · how you know it's scoped

The honest tell: the agent-risk lens caught something the policy lens shrugged at — or vice versa. Blend them and you'd miss it. In one team's worked example from the cookbook, a procurement-blocker thread read like routine billing all the way through; the only signal was a watched account name on a buried CC, and that match was what the policy lens caught while the risk lens was still shrugging. Blended lenses route it low-priority and miss it.

And the negative test: if every row came back compliant or violating and none came back "I can't tell," you forced false confidence. The third row exists precisely because a non-deterministic system produces ambiguity — hiding it is the failure.

Illustrative · one team

The procurement-blocker example — and the rough shape of "about five 'I can't tell' threads a week, a few of them the most important" — is one pseudonymised team's experience as told in the cookbook (a B2B SaaS support team), illustrative of the shape, not a benchmark or a rate to expect.

Why
The principle

Certainty about agent safety is a fantasy. The discipline is running the check — not waiting for it to come back clean.

"A scoped agent isn't one with no risk. It's one whose residual risk is named, owned, and visible to the next session."

None of this is exotic to a regulated firm. Normal security work already carries residual-risk vocabulary, accepted-risk registers, named owners — every SVP in a Nordic bank or insurer has met the concept. Agent security inherits all of it and adds three things on top: non-determinism, unbounded text inputs, and emergent tool use. You never get a proof. You get a loop.

Most teams stall right here — they treat the absent clean report as a blocker instead of treating the named residual as the deliverable. One footnote on the vocabulary: STRIDE shows up only as historical background — adapted from Microsoft's SDL, not used as the audit's scaffold here. R4 names the attack classes directly on purpose, so the lens can't collapse into closed-loop self-grading.

"I can't tell" is a valid agent output — and usually the most valuable one.
Where it sits · personal → company

This is the foundation guardrail layer. Run on your own agents, the check needs no permission — but its output travels: the named-residual report plus the CLAUDE.md rule are exactly what let a CTO put agents near regulated company systems with a documented, inheritable risk position instead of an unprovable promise of safety. Scope-for-trust is what every higher-autonomy and company-wide deployment rests on — the prerequisite for earning the next autonomy rung, and the boundary the whole organisation stops re-arguing once it's on record.

Context & Guardrails
Recipe · software · Context & Guardrails · the move before any agent fix

Write the failing test first

The principle: claims aren't evidence — an agent's "fixed it" is a story; a red-then-green test is the only thing that can't confabulate.

Before the agent touches code, make it write the test that fails for the bug's reason — watch it go red — then let it fix until the test goes green. The personal habit fences the agent's fluency at your own keyboard, and the same test becomes the gate every later PR has to clear.

A green diff is a confident claim. A test that went red first is the only proof the bug existed.
The mechanism · claim vs. evidence

Two paths from the same bug.

Hand a coding agent a bug and it does the natural thing: reads the symptom, nods, and starts editing — fast, plausible, unverified. The diff that comes back reads right. It compiles. It probably even runs. And that is exactly the trap, because a fix that reads right is not a fix that is right, and the agent's fluency is most convincing precisely where it's wrong. Its self-report — "fixed it, here's why" — is a reconstruction after the fact, not an observation. You are one "looks fine" away from merging a change whose only proof is that it didn't error.

The same bug can take a second path that ends somewhere very different. Before any code changes, the agent writes the test that reveals the bug, runs it, and you watch it fail — red, for the reason you'd expect. Then it fixes the root cause and runs again — green. Same input, same agent. The only thing that changed is that one path produced an artefact that could have said no. A test that fails first and passes after can't confabulate: it either reproduces the bug or it doesn't. The picture below puts the two paths side by side.

Process diagram · 01Same bug, same agent. Path B produced a test that could have said no — which is the entire difference between a claim and evidence.

The instruction is one sentence, and the order inside it is the whole pattern: write the test that reveals this bug, run it, confirm it fails the way you'd expect, then fix the root cause and run again. The middle clause does the work. A test that fails for the wrong reason is worse than no test — it green-lights with a typo in the assertion, a wrong import, a fixture that never reached the code. So you watch the red, and you check it's red because the bug is real, not because the test is broken. Only then is the green meaningful.

A test that fails for the wrong reason is worse than none. Watch the red — and check why it's red.

Resist the urge to dress this up. On a trivial bug, plan mode is overhead, not safety — ceremony you reach for because it feels like rigour. The discipline that actually earns its keep on a small bug isn't a plan; it's the failing test. And the temptation runs the other way too: when the fix is "obvious" you want to skip the test entirely. Obvious is exactly when the agent's guess compiles and ships. The smaller and more boring the bug, the cheaper the test, and the more often you'd otherwise wave it through on a glance.

The upgrade · rubber-stamp → interrogated

From the 30-second nod to the diff you argued with.

Writing the test is half the move; reading the diff is the other half, and it's a separate discipline. The brittle version is the rubber-stamp — the agent shows a change, you say "looks fine" in under thirty seconds, and you've tested the agent's confidence, not the code. The upgraded version is interrogated: you read the diff line by line, quote the one line you'd have written differently and say why, and let the better argument win — yours or the agent's. Then you push once on depth: is this the root cause, or a layer above it? The first cut usually fixes whatever makes the test pass; the deeper cut asks whether the test pointed at the right thing at all. Ask what a deeper edit would touch, and watch what the agent defends.

Process diagram · 02The accept upgrades from a glance to an argument: read · quote one line · push on root-cause-vs-surface · optional second pass on the deeper layer.

One trap is built into the loop itself. An agent under pressure to go green can write a test that passes vacuously — asserting nothing, or asserting something that was already true. It looks like coverage; it covers nothing. The guard is the same red you already insisted on: the test must fail first, and fail for the bug's reason. If it's green on the very first run, you didn't gain a test — you gained a decoration. This is why "watch it fail" isn't a nicety; it's the one check that catches a faked test before it becomes permanent false comfort in the suite.

The compounding loop · the suite gets richer

The test you wrote today catches the regression you'd re-debug next month.

Here's where the move stops being a one-off and starts paying interest. Each closed loop — bug, failing test, fix, passing test — leaves the test behind as permanent regression cover. The next change runs against it for free. Do this a hundred times and the suite isn't a chore you maintain; it's a hundred bugs that can no longer come back without tripping an alarm. The loop closes back through the codebase, not as a ritual you perform — the test you wrote for today's confident-but-wrong fix is the one that catches the silent regression you'd otherwise re-debug, from scratch, next month.

Process diagram · 03Compound interest on a test suite. Each closed loop leaves a test behind; the bug you fenced today can't come back without tripping an alarm.
Use when

You're about to hand an agent a bug and it's already drafting the fix — a backlog bug you half-remember, a wrong-total or off-by-one you can't eyeball, a change touching a file you didn't write. Anywhere agent speed outruns your ability to check it.

Build

A failing test committed before the fix — the bug's evidence, now permanent regression cover — and a shipped PR whose history shows test-before-fix, plus a diff you objected to at least once.

Test

The test went red before green, for the right reason.
Not "looks fine" in 30 seconds.

Core moves

The action, in order

Reuse it on every bug an agent offers to fix — not just this one.
1

Test first — and watch it fail

One line: write the test, run it, confirm it's red for the bug's reason.

2

Skip plan mode

On a trivial bug, ceremony is overhead. Tests-first is the discipline.

3

Read the diff, push one line

Quote the line you'd write differently. Better argument wins.

4

Push once on depth

Root cause, or a layer above? See what the agent defends.

5

Guard against faked tests

Green on first run = a decoration. It must fail first.

bug→failing test (red)→fix root cause→green→stays as regression cover

Then it's a habit, not a task: compound interest on a test suite. Each loop fences one more bug for good — and converts the agent's fluency from a risk into reviewable evidence.

Monday move: take the next bug an agent offers to fix. Before it touches code, send one line — "Write the failing test that proves this bug exists, run it, show me it fails — then fix the root cause." Needs nothing but a different first sentence: no platform, no budget, no sign-off. No test infra on this path? Log "no verifier here" as a real finding — the gap surfaces later, it isn't a blocker now.

Why
The principle

Claims aren't evidence. The agent's fix is a hypothesis; the failing test is the only thing that makes it falsifiable.

"Without a failing test first, the fix isn't a fix — it's a guess that happens to compile."

An agent's self-report is a reconstruction — persuasive precisely where it's wrong. A test that fails first and passes after is the one artefact in the loop that can't confabulate. It either reproduces the bug or it doesn't. You already know TDD; the second discipline is what's new — running it with an agent means the test also fences the agent, converting its fluency from a risk you absorb into evidence you can review.

The counterintuitive part: on a trivial bug you're tempted to skip the test because the fix is "obvious." Obvious is exactly when the agent's guess compiles and ships. Calibration helps here too — the curriculum's rule-of-thumb is to assume roughly a tenth of what the agent says or does is misrepresentation. The failing test is how you stop guessing which tenth.

⚠ Calibration, not measurement

"Assume ~10% of what the agent says or does is misrepresentation" is an illustrative calibration figure the curriculum uses to set skepticism — not a measured error rate. Could be more, could be less. It justifies the habit; it doesn't quantify the risk.

A green diff is a claim. A red-then-green test is evidence.
How you KNOW it worked · in practice

The test went red before it went green — you watched it fail for the right reason, not pass on the first run. A line-level objection sits in your scrollback or the commit body before the merge: proof you read the diff, not skimmed it. And the root-cause turn actually happened — a "is this the root cause or a layer above?" exchange before any commit.

The negative test is the honest one: if the agent's first answer went straight to green and you said "looks fine" in under thirty seconds, you tested the agent's confidence, not the code. No red, no objection, no depth question — no evidence.

Context & Guardrails
Recipe · software · Context & Guardrails · the read that earns the approval

Two reads, one approval

The principle: one kind of scrutiny catches one kind of miss — a human read and an agent's branch-walk catch different things.

Before you approve an agent's plan for a multi-file change, give it two different kinds of scrutiny — your situated read for the soft item only you can feel, and a second agent's branch-walk for everything you'd never hold in working memory — because neither read alone is complete.

The plan didn't get better because you stared harder. It got read twice, two different ways.
The mechanism · why one read isn't enough

Two reads, two different misses.

Start with the honest tell, because everyone recognises it: when was the last time an agent wrote a plan you approved without really reading? We all do it. The plan touches three files, lists verification steps, reads like a decision — and the approve button is right there while you're on a tight slot. The trap isn't laziness, it's structure. A seven-item plan with headers looks like a decision even when it's still a draft. Structure is persuasive; that's exactly what makes it dangerous at the approval prompt.

The fix isn't reading harder. It's reading twice, two different ways, because a single pass can only ever catch one shape of mistake. Your read is shallow but situated — you don't hold the whole design tree in your head, but you can feel the soft item, the assumption that's wrong for this repo, the file that shouldn't be touched at all. A second agent's walk-down is the inverse: exhaustive but unsituated — it surfaces every unresolved branch in the design, including the dozen you'd never have kept in working memory, but it has no nose for which one would quietly break your codebase. Below is the picture.

Process diagram · 01Two reads, drawn as two catch-fields. They overlap on the obvious; the gap on each side is what the other read alone would have missed.

The non-overlap is the whole reason you run both. Your read carries voice-of-experience the agent's breadth can't fake: you've seen what happens when the auth helper gets edited for a feature that had nothing to do with auth. The agent has never shipped your code at 5pm on a Friday. The walk-down, meanwhile, carries a completeness you can't match by squinting — it will dredge up the nullable-id question, the cache-or-live question, the retry-path question, one at a time, until it runs out of branches. Pair the two and you get a complete read. Run either alone and you've shipped a draft you mistook for a decision.

Assumption-silent isn't assumption-free. Every plan assumes something; the good ones say what.

The upgrade · rubber-stamp → paired read

From the sixty-second nod to a gate the plan has to cross.

The default move is a rubber-stamp: a plan approved in under a minute on a single glance, where the structure did the persuading and your read added nothing. The upgrade is the same approval prompt run as a deliberate two-pass gate. First, push back with what only you can see — and do it specifically. Pick keep planning with feedback, find one step, and quote its number and a word from it: not "looks good, one concern," but "step 3 — 'update the auth helper' — that's the wrong file for this change." A quote forces the agent to revise the actual step instead of nodding at a vague worry. Then run the second read. Below: the nod on the left, the gate on the right.

Process diagram · 02The approval is the same button. What changed is the gate the plan crosses to reach it — a quoted push-back, then a branch-walk run to exhaustion.

Two things break the gate if you skip them. The first: the agent will say "good point" and re-soften the same step in the revised plan. An acknowledgement is not a fix. Check the regenerated step — if it re-softened, push again, same quote. The second: run the walk-down as a Q-and-A sequence, not a one-shot dump. Ask the agent to walk the design tree it didn't resolve, branch by branch, one question with a recommended answer each, and let it run until it's out of branches — you don't get to decide it's finished early. A prompt that returns every branch in one list is a list; a sequence that resolves them one at a time is a read.

The compounding loop · the plan-reading gets cheaper

Each pass pre-shapes the next plan in this repo.

Here's the counterintuitive part, and it's also where the move stops being a chore. This feels expensive — two reads on every plan? — but it's cheaper than it looks, for two reasons. One: you don't have to execute a plan to know it's good. Making the plan good is the work; the running is just typing. Two: the branch that sharpened how plans get made here doesn't evaporate when you approve. The same wrong-for-this-repo assumption your push-back caught becomes a saved rule, and the next plan in this repo arrives pre-shaped by it — fewer soft items, fewer unresolved branches, less pushing-back to land. The loop below shows it closing.

Process diagram · 03The branch your push-back surfaced gets saved as a rule — and the next plan in this repo arrives pre-shaped, so the reading gets cheaper each pass.
What "Test" actually means · the negative check

If you can't name what your read caught, the two reads collapsed into one.

The clean test isn't "did I approve a plan." It's "can I prove it got two distinct kinds of scrutiny." The scrollback should show a keep-planning message quoting a specific step number and a word from it — not "looks good, one concern." It should show a Q-and-A branch-walk that ran to exhaustion, not a single dumped list. At least one walk-down recommendation should have been rejected and corrected for this codebase — the recommendations are defaults, not prescriptions. And the honest negative test: name one thing your push-back caught that the agent's walk-down would have missed. If you can't, the two reads collapsed into one — the agent did both passes and your situated read added nothing. That's the failure mode hiding behind a clean approval.

Use when

An agent hands you a clean-looking plan for a multi-file change and the approve button is right there — the work is non-trivial enough that touching the wrong file matters, and the plan's confidence outruns your actual read of it.

Build

An approved plan file that carries both reads in its history — the gates you read, the soft items your push-back hardened, the branches the walk-down resolved. Note the path: it's the input to the next phase.

Test

You can name one thing your push-back caught the walk-down would have missed.
If you can't — the two reads collapsed into one.

Core moves

The action, in sequence

Each move is built to catch a different kind of miss.
1

Read it as three artefacts

File list, verification steps, named assumptions — separately, not one wall.

2

Push back with a quote

Quote a step number and a word. The soft item only you can see.

3

Check it sharpened

Don't accept a nod. If it re-softened, push again.

4

Walk down the branches

One question at a time, to exhaustion. You don't call it done.

5

Reject one, then approve

Defaults, not prescriptions. Then stop — you don't execute.

read→push back→walk down→approve→save the branch as a rule

The branch that sharpened plan-making here gets saved, and the next plan arrives pre-shaped. Making the plan good is the work — you don't have to execute it to know it's good.

Monday move: next plan an agent hands you, don't approve it. Keep planning with feedback · quote one step + one word · then walk the branches one at a time · reject one · approve. No platform, no budget, no sign-off — push-back is a chat message, the walk-down is a prompt, all inside one session on a task already in your backlog.

Why
The principle

One kind of scrutiny catches one kind of miss. Pair two, and the gap between them is where the plan-reading skill lives.

"Plan mode makes the read possible; it isn't the read."

The mechanism is plain once you name it. Your read is shallow but situated — you feel the soft item, the assumption that's wrong for this repo, the file that shouldn't be touched. The agent's walk-down is exhaustive but unsituated — it surfaces every branch in the design tree, including the ones you'd never have held in working memory. Reading a plan is finite; pair the two and you get a complete read. Neither alone does.

And it's cheaper than it feels, because you don't have to execute a plan to know it's good — the approval is the work, not the running. Assumption-silent isn't assumption-free. Every plan assumes something, and the good ones say what; the two reads are how the silent assumptions get named before they cost you a file.

The structure persuaded you. Two reads is how you stop letting it.
Where it sits · personal → team → company

This is the personal foundation of Context & Guardrails — the read-discipline an individual practises at the approval prompt. It doesn't stay personal. The same branch a second read surfaces is what a team later hardens into a shared judge or a CI check that catches it before any teammate has to ask — so that the company's plan-quality stops depending on whether each individual happened to read twice. The habit you build on one plan is the seed of a gate the whole org rests on. (Positioning, not a coined law.)

Context & Guardrails
Recipe · Context & Guardrails · software lane · the first move before STRIDE

Map the access surface first

The principle: Map what you're protecting before you name what could go wrong.

Before you threat-model, send a fresh subagent to walk the whole feature and map who can reach what — so your own attention stays free for the two surfaces only you can name: the one it under-weighted, and the one it missed. Breadth is borrowed; judgment is yours.

The breadth is borrowed. The two amber threads are yours — the surface it drew too thin, and the one it never drew.
The mechanism · why you map before you threat-model

STRIDE has nothing to chew on until the surface is mapped.

Here's the trap, and almost everyone walks into it: you've a feature shipping this week — a webhook handler, a new route, a tenant-scoped query — a staff engineer and a CISO will review it, and you're quietly nervous one of them will catch a surface you didn't think to look at. So you reach for STRIDE, the six-category threat checklist. That's the trap. STRIDE without a surface map is pub-quiz threat-modelling — six categories walked against a vibe. The thing you're missing isn't the threat list; it's the map of what the threats land on. You can't reason about spoofing a boundary you never wrote down.

So map first. But mapping every entry point, boundary, data tier and auth checkpoint a feature touches is a long, structured breadth read — and breadth reads are exactly what you hand to a fresh subagent. Invoke a curated access-control skill, name the feature by route or a couple of symbols, and let it find the code itself. It burns its whole context window walking the tree; yours stays clean for the judgment only you carry. This is the breadth-first-to-a-subagent split: the wall of structured output leaves the main thread on purpose, and you stay rested for the part a generic reader structurally can't do. Below, the same feature read twice — once wide, once deep.

Process diagram · 01Same feature, two readers. Breadth from the skill, depth from you — they converge on the delta note, and that join is what STRIDE reads.

Make the read cover six surfaces, not five: entry points · trust boundaries crossed (service, network, tenant, role) · data read and written with its sensitivity tier · authorization checkpoints, separated into present, assumed, and delegated · external tool and connector calls · and the load-bearing one — anything that bypasses, defers, or inherits an auth decision made elsewhere. That last category is where the surprises live. A generic reader handles standard middleware well and hand-rolled auth badly; it reads explicit checkpoints well and inherited-elsewhere decisions worst of all — which is precisely where breaches actually breed.

A good curated skill doesn't pretend to omniscience — it narrates what it misses while it works. It flags that auth middleware on a parent router propagates to every route beneath it, so finding the handler but not where it's mounted under-reports protection. It flags implicit trust between internal services. It flags bespoke auth it reads worse than the standard kind. Then it closes with a calibrated self-grade — its own read of how much it caught, not a measured accuracy and not a benchmark about the move — and names where the last percents hide. A flagged uncertainty is more useful than a confident fabrication. Those flagged spots aren't noise to skim past; they're invitations addressed to you.

The skill reads standard middleware well and the weird bits badly. The weird bits are where the breaches live.

The upgrade · vibe-check → mapped surface

From threat-modelling a vibe to threat-modelling a map.

The upgrade is the same shape as every guardrail move: from something ephemeral and felt to something explicit and durable. On the left below, STRIDE walked against a remembered, hand-waved surface — "I think auth's fine" — six categories floating over nothing. That's the pub-quiz. On the right, STRIDE walked against an explicit six-surface map with the inherited-auth-bypass row lit up: defensible. Same six categories either way; the difference is entirely in whether they have a real surface to land on. The map is what turns a checklist into an analysis.

Process diagram · 02Same six categories, different ground. STRIDE over a vibe is a pub-quiz; STRIDE over a six-surface map is defensible.

Now the move you can't delegate. Read the map's confessed blind spots — don't skim them — and write the delta: two surfaces, each reasoned in this codebase's own terms. One the skill flagged harder than you would have (you'd under-weighted it). One you know matters that it missed — usually the part you'd call "the weird bit," where a generic pass runs thinnest. Push every reason until it names something a different codebase wouldn't share. "The billing webhook re-hits the queue on retry, so the same event gets reprocessed" beats "webhooks need auth." The first is yours; the second is anyone's.

And the delta — not the skill's wall of output — is what you ship to STRIDE next. The raw map is the input to your judgment; the delta is the artifact. Add a one-line context header if a teammate landing cold would miss something the map quietly assumes. That's the whole handoff: not a hardening backlog, not a fix list, just a map with your fingerprints on the surfaces only you knew to check. The loop below shows where this goes once it's a habit — each feature you map widens the kit the next feature's read starts from.

Process diagram · 03The loop closes through the repo, not one perfect map. One hardening decision is enough — the surface you named becomes where the next feature's read starts.
What "Test" actually means · in practice

The test is both shapes present, neither generic.

You know the move worked when the delta note has both shapes present and neither is generic — an over-weighted surface and a missed one, each reasoned in terms a different codebase wouldn't share. A teammate could hand it to STRIDE cold and threat-model something real, not a thin map. The tell that you skimmed: if the skill caught nothing you'd have missed, either the feature is trivial or you rushed to the next prompt and never sat with the map. And the failing case is sharp — if the only output is the skill's raw map with no delta layered on, the breadth read shipped and your read didn't, so STRIDE will chew on a map with no judgment in it. The percent the skill prints is its own calibrated read of its coverage — not a measured accuracy, not a benchmark about the pattern — and you treat it as a pointer to where to look, never as proof the map is right.

Use when

You're shipping a feature with an external or user-facing surface this week, a staff engineer and a CISO will review it, and "I think the auth is fine" is doing more work than it should.

Build

A surface-map delta note — the skill's six-surface map, its confessed blind spots and self-grade, plus your two surfaces. Session scratch, deliberately ephemeral.

Test

Both shapes present, neither generic.
Not just the skill's raw map.

Core moves

The action, in sequence

What changes = who does the breadth read, and whose judgment owns the deltas.
1

Dispatch the surface read

Hand a subagent the feature by name. Let it find the code.

2

Cover six surfaces, not five

Including inherited-auth bypasses — where surprises live.

3

Read the blind spots

The flagged-uncertain spots are invitations, not noise.

4

Write the delta

One under-weighted, one missed — each codebase-specific.

5

Ship the delta, not the dump

The delta is the artifact STRIDE reads. Not the wall.

map a feature→name the delta→harden one surface→it joins the kit→repeat

Then it's a discipline, not a one-off: the kit's breadth grows across many features. One hardening decision is enough each pass — the next feature's read starts from the surface this one named.

Monday move: the feature you're closest to shipping. Name it in one sentence, ask Claude Code to run the access-control skill on it as a subagent — no file paths — then write two lines: one surface it flagged harder than you would have, one it missed that you know matters. Installs to ~/.claude/skills/ · read-only · no admin · no team rollout · before your next PR review.

Why
The principle

Map what you're protecting before you name what could go wrong.

"The skill does the breadth you wouldn't have. You name the surface only you could."

The competence was never in knowing the threats — it's in knowing what you're protecting, and refusing to let a generic reader's confidence stand in for your codebase's particulars. A curated skill packages upstream work you don't re-derive: invoke, don't re-derive. But it reads standard middleware well and hand-rolled, inherited-elsewhere auth worst of all — exactly the surfaces where breaches breed. So the labour splits by what each party is good at: the subagent does breadth on a fresh context, cheap and calibrated-honest about its blind spots; you do the codebase-specific depth it structurally cannot have.

Mapping before threat-modelling is the same discipline as writing the failing test before the fix — ground the work in what's true before you reason about what could go wrong. The reason a CISO signs off isn't that you ran a tool. It's that the map has your fingerprints on the surfaces only you knew to check.

Breadth is borrowed. Judgment is yours.
Where it sits

This is the first guardrail in the trust arc: paired with STRIDE and the ADR under pressure, it walks a single engineer into staff-engineer and CISO review with a defensible map, a hardening decision, and a named residual risk — personal competence, made reviewable. And that same map-the-boundary-before-the-build discipline is what scope-for-trust raises to company scope, where it becomes the precondition for an organisation trusting any agent it didn't personally calibrate. Map a feature's access surface here; scope an agent's surface to what the org can trust there — same move, two surfaces.

Context & Guardrails
Recipe · software lane · Context & Guardrails · personal → team → company

Name the threat before you build

The principle: threat modelling is only useful if it ends in a decision — STRIDE is the surface to reject most things against, not an oracle.

Before you harden anything, run STRIDE across a mapped surface, name the single worst realistic incident, pick the one threat that matches it, and write the call down as an ADR — so the worry becomes a defensible decision your whole team inherits instead of re-argues.

Fifteen rejected on purpose. The one you keep arrives with its alternatives already weighed.
The mechanism · what STRIDE actually chews on

STRIDE has nothing to chew on without a surface.

The most common way threat-modelling goes wrong is also the most innocent-looking: someone opens STRIDE and starts free-associating attacks against the code in their head. That's pub-quiz threat modelling — "STRIDE without an access-surface map is pub-quiz threat modeling." The six categories are a lens, not an oracle; a lens needs something to focus on. So the move starts one rung earlier: map the access surface first — run the access-control read as a subagent on the feature and you get a surface map, not a feeling. Who can reach what, through which checkpoint, under which trust boundary. Now STRIDE has a real object.

Then comes the part that feels backwards until you've done it once: you run all six categories expecting to reject most of them. Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information-disclosure, Denial-of-service, Elevation-of-privilege — fired at the mapped surface, the output has more entries than you want. That over-supply is the point. The structure exists so you can reject threats explicitly — acceptable risk, out of scope, already mitigated — which is exactly what makes the one you keep defensible. A threat held up against five it beat is an argument; a threat picked from thin air is a vibe. The diagram below shows the funnel: surface in, six lenses, many candidates, one decision out.

Process diagram · 01The surface feeds the six lenses; the lenses fan out into many candidates; the worst-realistic-incident story is the funnel that collapses them to one.

The funnel that collapses the candidates is not a scoring rubric — it's a story. Name the worst realistic incident, then the hardening decision is usually obvious. Not the most exotic attack; the one that would actually wake someone at 3am. For a billing webhook that re-hits the queue on retry, that story writes itself: a retry storm replays the event and double-charges a customer. Once the worst case is on the page, the threat you pick almost always falls out of it. And if your pick doesn't match the worst-case story, that's the tell — you optimised for the threat that's cheapest to fix, not the one that matters.

Pick one threat to harden, not five. If your pick doesn't match the worst-case story, you optimised for effort, not risk.

The upgrade · from a quiet worry to a written decision

The thing you're quietest about becomes the thing on the record.

Every engineer shipping a feature with an external surface carries one quiet unease — "I'm a bit nervous about that webhook." It's the bit you'd call "the weird bit": the endpoint trusting a header it shouldn't, the path that re-hits the queue on retry. The trap isn't ignorance — you know roughly where the risk lives. The trap is that nobody made the threat a written decision, so the staff engineer finds it in review, or the CISO finds it in prod, and the team re-argues it from scratch on the next feature that touches the same surface. The upgrade is to crystallise that unease into an ADR before the review, not after. Below: the faint thread of worry on the left, the durable artefact on the right.

Process diagram · 02The ADR is the artefact your CISO would actually read — one engineer briefing the next, not a reviewer's checkbox.

What you write down is deliberately small: one ADR per hardening decision, in whatever convention your repo already uses for decisions (default docs/adr/NNNN-slug.md). Four sections — Context, Decision, Alternatives considered, Constraint. The rejected STRIDE threats live in Alternatives considered with the reason each was rejected; the rest of the STRIDE output stays alongside as evidence, not as a hardening backlog you've quietly committed yourself to. And note what the ADR is not: it sits on disk, discoverable and named, but it does not auto-load into every future session the way a rules file does. It's read when someone explicitly reaches for it — which is exactly the right weight for a decision, heavy enough to inherit, light enough not to nag.

One more honesty clause: STRIDE is a tool, not the law. If its six categories were the wrong lens for this feature — if the real risk is abuse-case or insider-threat shaped — say so in Alternatives considered and reason in the lens that actually fit. The skill gives you breadth fast; the codebase-specific judgement is yours to add. A mnemonic that catches most attack shapes is not a guarantee you caught yours.

The compounding loop · one feature thickens the team's posture

Each ADR is the precedent the next threat-model starts from.

The diagram below shows why one defensible call is worth more than its single feature. Map the surface, run STRIDE, reject most, write the ADR — then the loop closes back onto the next feature's surface map, and the team's ADR folder is visibly thicker each pass. One hardening decision is enough per feature; the team kit's breadth grows across many features. The fourth time someone threat-models a surface like the billing webhook, they don't start from zero — they start from the precedent the last engineer left. That's the difference between a security review that re-discovers the same threats every quarter and one that inherits them.

Process diagram · 03The folder thickens, the re-arguing stops. One defensible call per feature; the company's posture is the sum of the ADRs nobody has to re-derive.
What "Test" actually means · how you know the threat was named

A listed threat is not a named one.

The trap at the finish line is mistaking a long STRIDE list for a decision. So the test is falsifiable, and it runs on the artefact itself. First: the ADR's Context — or the scrollback — should show the worst-case story preceded the threat pick. Worst case first, then the choice. Reversed order is menu-shopping, and it reads as reversed. Second: Alternatives considered names at least two rejected threats with a real reason each — acceptable risk, already mitigated, out of scope — not left dangling as backlog. Third, the sharpest tell: if the ADR could have been written without ever running the surface map, STRIDE was performative. The map's codebase-specific surfaces should be visible in the reasoning. A decision that reads like it came from a generic checklist probably did.

Use when

You're shipping a feature with a surface a teammate could miss in review — a new webhook, a public read, an action the agent now takes for a user — and "we'll secure it later" is doing the deciding.

Build

One ADR per hardening decision — Context · Decision · Alternatives considered · Constraint. The rejects live in Alternatives; the rest of the STRIDE output stays as evidence.

Test

The worst-case story precedes the pick; ≥2 threats rejected with reasons.
Not a list someone will harden later.

Core moves

The action, in sequence

An unbounded worry becomes one written, defensible call.
1

Map the surface first

Run the access-control read as a subagent. STRIDE has nothing to chew on without it.

2

Run all six, expect to reject

Fire STRIDE at the map. The over-supply is the point.

3

Name the worst case, pick one

One worst realistic incident. One threat that matches it.

4

Write it as an ADR

Context · Decision · Alternatives · Constraint. The rejects are the evidence.

map surface→run STRIDE→reject most→write ADR→next feature

Then it's the team's habit, not one engineer's: each ADR is a precedent the next threat-model starts from. The folder thickens; the security review stops re-arguing the same surfaces.

Monday move: pick one feature you're shipping this week with an external surface. Vanilla Claude Code · access-control read as a subagent, then STRIDE on what it surfaces · name the one worst incident · four sentences saved where your repo keeps decisions. Nothing here needs sign-off, budget, or a platform — you arrive at review with the call already made.

Why
The principle

Threat modelling is only useful if it ends in a decision. STRIDE is the surface you reject against — not an oracle.

"The ADR is the one thing your CISO will actually read."

STRIDE's real gift isn't catching everything — it's giving you a structured surface to reject most things against, so the one threat you harden arrives with its alternatives already weighed. That's the difference between a defensible architectural call and a vibe. The mechanism is the write: a decision made under named pressure converts a private worry into shared, inheritable context. Most teams skip the write — so the same threat gets re-argued on every feature that touches the same surface.

The name is honest about its limits. STRIDE — coined by Loren Kohnfelder and Praerit Garg in a 1999 Microsoft threat-modelling memo, later sharpened by Adam Shostack in Threat Modeling: Designing for Security (2014) — is a mnemonic for the six ways a system gets attacked, not a guarantee you caught yours. A threat you haven't named is one the whole team re-discovers, one expensive review at a time. Naming it once, in writing, is the cheapest insurance in the building.

A listed threat is a chore. A named one is a decision.
Context & Guardrails
Recipe · software lane · the move after a hardening call

Write the decision before you forget why

The principle: context as standing input — a decision that lives only in your head is invisible to every session that follows.

The instant a real architectural call resolves under pressure, write the four lines that capture it — context, decision, alternatives, and the one constraint that picked the winner — into a repo-resident record, while the why is still warm and free. layer: personal→team→company · phase: Context & Guardrails

The decision was real. The why evaporated — except the one line you wrote down.
The mechanism · two fates of the same decision

The choosing was cheap. Loading the context was the expensive part.

A threat-model pass flags one thing worth hardening. You weigh the trade-off, pick a side, ship the fix, and move on with the small relief of being past it. The relief is the trap. It feels like a decision banked — but the only thing you actually kept is the feeling of having decided, and a feeling is not an artefact. The reasoning that made one option obviously right was a whole loaded context: the attacker you were picturing, the alternative you rejected and why, the constraint that broke the tie. That context decays fast and silently. A week later someone in review asks "why this and not the obvious alternative?" and you find yourself reconstructing a rationale you no longer actually hold — or worse, defending a guess.

In an agentic workflow the decay costs twice. The agent that picks up adjacent work next week has no memory of the room where you decided. It reads the repo cold, sees a settled trade-off with no recorded reason, and does the rational thing: it re-litigates the call from scratch — sometimes landing on the option you already rejected, for the exact reason you already rejected it. The diagram below shows the fork: same decision, two fates, split only by whether the constraint got written down while it was warm.

Process diagram · 01Same input, different output — because the context was captured, not lost. The fork is one four-line file.

Here's the counterintuitive bit. The expensive thing to preserve isn't what you decided — anyone can read the diff and see that you chose option X. The expensive thing is the constraint that made X obvious at the time. That single line is the test by which a future reader knows whether your call still holds when the inputs change. "We chose the stricter token scope because the endpoint is reachable unauthenticated" ages gracefully — the day the endpoint goes behind auth, anyone can see the call is now reversible. Strip the constraint and all that survives is a verdict with no expiry date, defended forever by reflex because nobody remembers what would falsify it.

A decision you can't reconstruct isn't a decision you still own — it's a guess you'll re-make under worse conditions.

The shelf-life upgrade · from private judgment to repo record

From the thought you'll keep to the file the agent reads cold.

The move is not "document more." It's a shelf-life upgrade on a single decision: take the rationale that currently lives as a fading thought — "I'll remember why" — and turn it into a numbered file the repo carries forward. The convention most teams reach for is an Architecture Decision Record: a short, standalone, repo-resident note, one per decision, numbered so they read as a history. Four labelled sections do the work — context · decision · alternatives · constraint — with the constraint section as the load-bearing one. Not a wiki page that rots in a corner, not a Slack thread that scrolls away, not a commit message buried in history. A file that the next session — yours or an agent's — cold-reads as part of the system's standing context.

Default convention

The path docs/adr/NNNN-slug.md and the four-section shape (context · decision · alternatives · constraint) are an illustrative default, not a mandate. Your repo's actual ADR path and section shape override it — if the team already has a convention, use theirs. The portable part is the discipline, not the directory name.

Process diagram · 02Private judgment → repo-resident, agent-readable record. The constraint section is the one that ages well. Path and sections shown are the default convention — yours override.

One ADR is a note. A repo of them is a different thing entirely — it's the layer the next decision rests on instead of fighting against. Each pass thickens the docs/adr/ directory, and each new constraint is read as standing context by whatever reads the repo next: a reviewer, a junior who wasn't in the room, a memory pass that loads prior decisions, or an agent doing adjacent work. The decision-recall doesn't depend on the person who made the call still being available — or still remembering. The loop below closes through the repo: decide, write the constraint warm, the directory accretes, the next session inherits the why, and decides the next thing on top of it rather than against it.

Process diagram · 03The next agent inherits the why. Each pass the docs/adr/ directory thickens — and the org's architectural reasoning starts living in the codebase, not in senior heads.
Use when

You just made a real architectural call under pressure — a STRIDE pass picked a threat to harden, a curated skill surfaced a trade-off and you committed — and the only record is the relief you're past it. Or you catch yourself saying "we decided that already" and can't point at where.

Build

A standalone, numbered, repo-resident record — docs/adr/NNNN-slug.md by default (your repo's convention wins) — with four sections: context, decision, alternatives, and the constraint that picked the winner.

Test

A teammate reads it and says "right, that's why."
Not a stranger's "well-formatted."

Core moves

The action, in sequence

Ninety seconds while the why is still warm — not a process to roll out.
1

Catch it the moment it lands

The trigger is the felt "okay, we're hardening this" — not a calendar slot. An hour later it's a reconstruction.

2

Write four things, not a treatise

Context, decision, the alternatives you weighed, and the one constraint that picked the winner.

3

Put it where the repo travels

The team's ADR path, or default docs/adr/. Not a private note — part of the system you have.

4

Resist the compliance reading

A real trade-off written down is design. A fabricated one is paperwork — write only what you actually decided.

decide→write the constraint warm→repo accretes→next session inherits→repeat

Then it's a habit, not a chore: the why stops evaporating. Each constraint you bank is one the next reader — human or agent — never has to reconstruct.

Monday move: after your next real trade-off, stop for ninety seconds and write four lines into docs/adr/NNNN-slug.md (or wherever your repo keeps them) — context, call, the alternative you rejected, the constraint that decided it. An ADR is a markdown file in a directory you already own · no platform · no budget · no sign-off · ~90 sec. You're not proposing a process; you're writing down a decision you already made.

Why
The principle

Context as standing input. The ADR is the only channel by which a past judgment reaches a future agent.

"The expensive part of a decision was loading the context that made it obvious — and that context evaporates faster than the decision does."

The agent reading your repo has no memory of the room where you decided. A decision that lives only in your head is invisible to every session that follows — so the ADR isn't bureaucracy, it's the wire from a past judgment to a future reader. The constraint line is the highest-leverage sentence in the file: it's the test by which anyone later knows whether your call still holds when the inputs change. Strip it, and you've kept the verdict but lost the expiry date.

And the failure mode is specific. Treat the ADR as a checkbox after a menu-pick threat and you get paperwork — a fabricated trade-off written down to satisfy a form. The move is real only when the decision was real: name the worst thing the feature could do, find the threat adjacent to that answer, and record the constraint that resolved it. A genuine trade-off written down is design; a fabricated one is theatre.

A guess you'll re-make under worse conditions is not a decision you own.
Test · how you know it worked

The practitioner's "right, that's why" — the constraint line reconstructs the call without you in the room — beats a stranger's "well-formatted." Three more checks the file should survive: an agent picking up adjacent work builds on the constraint instead of re-deriving the settled trade-off; the four sections answer the hostile review question "why not the obvious alternative?" before it's asked; and the negative test — if the only record is that you feel past the decision, it didn't cross. Felt relief is not an artefact. Reconstructing the why a week later means the move never happened.

Context & Guardrails
Recipe · software · Context & Guardrails · the first long send-off

Walk the system against the task

The principle: the system you have is what gets tested — not the one you meant to build.

Take the context you've accumulated, walk it against the one real task you're about to send off, fill only the worst few gaps, and let the agent run against your system as it stands — so the return teaches you what's actually missing, not what you imagined. This is a personal habit that keeps a whole company's memory honest at scale.

You didn't patch the system clean. You load-tested it — filled the worst three, left two open on purpose, pinned the SHA, let it run.
The mechanism · what a real task makes visible

A gap is invisible until a specific load walks over it.

You already have a context system. Not a tidy one — a CLAUDE.md, a CLAUDE.local.md, a folder of observations, an ADR or two, a skill you authored last week. Each was written in its own moment, to fix the thing in front of you that day, and none of it was ever measured against the task you're about to send off. Read cold, the pile looks ready. That's the illusion: completeness is a property a context system only appears to have until something real leans on it.

The shorter loops sit behind you — a bug fix, a plan read, work where you stayed in the loop. This is the first long one: multi-hour, sustained, running without you watching. And the move that decides whether it's worth your while isn't writing more rules. It's walking the system you have against the system the task needs and seeing, for the first time, which lines are load-bearing for this work and which slots are simply empty. The files don't change in the walk — the task does the X-raying. The diagram below is the same pile twice: ready-looking on top, X-rayed by one named task on the bottom.

Process diagram · 01The files didn't change — the task did the X-raying. A gap is only visible against a specific load.

Walking is a job you can hand to a subagent. Point one at your CLAUDE.md + CLAUDE.local.md + memory + ADRs + any skills and connectors, and have it walk them against what this task needs. It returns a ranked gap list. The trap here is reverence: the audit is a hypothesis about your system's holes, not a verdict you clear. Push back on it exactly the way you'd interrogate any read — it over-weights the tidy gaps it can name and misses the assumption baked so deep nobody wrote it down. You're the one who knows which hole will actually hurt this run.

Walk the system you have against the system the task needs. The empty slot is the gap.

The discipline · over-prepared loses to deliberately under-filled

Fill the worst three. Then stop on purpose.

Here's where almost everyone's instinct fails them. The audit hands you five gaps and every nerve says close them all — give the agent its best shot. Resist it. Fill the worst three; leave the rest open, and write down which two you're leaving and why. The skipped gaps aren't laziness — they're the instrumentation. A system patched until it looks complete can't tell you what it was missing, because you erased the evidence before running the test. Under-filling on purpose is what lets the return surface what genuinely breaks. The diagram below draws the two paths to a send-off, and which one actually teaches.

Process diagram · 02Patch it clean and the return goes quiet. Under-fill on purpose and the run breaks where you can read it. Three is a deliberate teaching budget for the experiment — not a measured rule.

One trap is sharp enough to name on its own. You'll spot a thin place, decide "that's a real code change, I'll skip it," and the un-packaged run fails in a boring way — wrong DB assumption, stale config — instead of an interesting one. If the audit calls it context, it's context, even when the fill is just one rule ("we use Postgres, not Mongo"). A boring failure teaches nothing; the agent lost coherence on something you'd have caught in ten seconds. The whole point of the run is the interesting break — the one only the next move can diagnose. Don't defer a contextual gap because the fill looks architectural.

Then send it off un-packaged, in the same session: no plan.md, no verifier, no reference artefact. Pin the starting point first — commit current state on a feature branch, record the SHA and the transcript path — then dispatch the scoped task with your rules, memory, ADRs and skills loaded, and let it run. One caveat has to travel with that word: un-packaged here is a deliberate first step to expose failure modes — packaging is the right move once you've seen what un-packaged gets wrong, not a thing to skip. You're not shipping a production run you owe a clean result. You're running an experiment. The trace is the data.

The compounding loop · evidence over anticipation

Each lap, the gaps you fill are the ones real runs surfaced.

The picture below closes the thread. Scope one task, walk the system as an audit, push back and pick the worst three, fill those and pin the SHA, send it off un-packaged, read the return, then sharpen the gaps the run actually exposed — and scope the next task. Each pass the context carries a richer, evidence-fed system, and the holes you close are the ones a real load found, not the ones you imagined at the desk. That's the difference between a habit that compounds and a policy nobody's work ever validated.

Process diagram · 03Compound on evidence, not anticipation. Each lap the gaps you fill are the ones real runs surfaced — not the ones you imagined.
What "Test" actually means · in practice

The honest test is the gap you can name out loud.

You'll know the move worked not by a green check but by what you can say. You can name the one task in a sentence, and its 'done' is concrete — neither a typo-fix nor a quarter-long epic. The audit returned a ranked list and you picked exactly the worst few, filled those, and can say out loud which gaps you're deliberately leaving open and why. At least one fill was a contextual gap you were tempted to defer as "architectural" — you filled it anyway, even if the fill was one rule. And the starting point is pinned: git log shows a feature branch with a "starting point" commit before the agent's first task commit, with the SHA and transcript path noted somewhere you'll find later. The negative test is the tell: if you closed every gap you could find, you over-prepared and the return will teach you nothing; if you packaged it, you pre-empted the lesson. The un-packaged failure is the data.

Use when

A real send-off task is in front of you — a migration, a gnarly refactor, a test-coverage expansion, an API cutover — and you don't actually know whether the context you've built will carry it, or where it'll quietly fall through.

Build

A load-tested context system pinned to a comparable starting point: two or three run-tied fills, a business-rules pointer wired or the gap named, a starting-point commit at a recorded SHA — plus the running task itself.

Test

You can name the gaps you left open and why.
Not a system patched until it looks complete.

Core moves

The action, in sequence

Your files, your repo, one session — no platform, no sign-off.
1

Scope one real send-off

A slice with a 'done' you can say in a sentence. Not an epic, not a typo.

2

Walk it as a subagent audit

Point a subagent at your files. Then push back on what it ranks.

3

Fill the worst three

Three is the budget, not a minimum. Skip the rest on purpose.

4

Don't defer the "architectural" one

If the audit calls it context, it's context — fill it.

5

Pin the SHA, send un-packaged

Commit on a branch, note the SHA, let it run as it stands.

scope→walk as audit→fill worst 3→pin · send un-packaged→read the return→sharpen

Then it's a habit, not a heroic prep: the gaps you fill are the ones real runs surfaced. Each lap the system carries a richer, evidence-fed load — the move you reuse before every long send-off, forever.

Monday move: pick one task off your backlog you've meant to send an agent. Point a subagent at your CLAUDE.md · CLAUDE.local.md · observations · ADRs — have it rank the gaps against that task. Fill the worst three, write down the two you're leaving, commit on a feature branch, note the SHA, send it off un-packaged. Your repo · your files · one session · no platform · no budget · no one's sign-off.

Why
The principle

The system you have is what gets tested — not the one you meant to build.

"Fill the worst three; send the rest un-packaged — the gap you leave open is the one the run will teach you."

Every instinct says prepare thoroughly: close every hole the audit finds, give the agent its best shot. But a system patched until it looks complete can't tell you what it was missing, because you erased the evidence before running the test. Gap analysis is walking the system you have against the system the task needs — and the only honest way to find the gap is to let the real load find it for you.

The trap inside the trap is the contextual gap dressed as architecture. Defer it and the run fails boringly, on a wrong assumption you'd have caught in seconds — which teaches nothing — instead of failing interestingly, where the agent loses coherence in a way only the next move can diagnose. Treat the send-off as an experiment, not a production run you owe a clean result. The trace is the data.

Filling fewer gaps teaches you more.
Read these as labelled, not literal

"Three" is a deliberate teaching budget for a first un-packaged run — not a measured optimum. The point is to under-fill on purpose so the run can teach you; there's no law that filling three gaps maximises learning.

"Un-packaged" is a sequencing choice, not a claim that un-packaged runs are better — it's a deliberate first step to expose failure modes. Packaging is the right move once you've seen what un-packaged gets wrong, not a thing to skip.

The three-block frame the walk leans on — Huryn's three-block memory — travels as a frame for naming what you've already built, not a template to fill in. It makes an empty slot legible; it is not a checklist to author against.

Where this sits · personal → team → company

This is the personal-layer habit that keeps a context system honest at scale. An individual who walks and deliberately under-fills produces evidence-fed gaps instead of imagined ones — and that same discipline, test against a real load and fill from what the run exposed, is exactly what keeps a team's shared kit and a company's memory layer growing from real failures rather than prophylactic policy no one's load ever validated. The un-packaged failure here is also the prerequisite that teaches what the next move — packaging the run — has to carry.

The Work
The Work
Recipe · business lane · phase: The Work · the more-than-one-mind move

Split the work across agents

The principle: the filesystem is the meeting room — parallel agents coordinate through files you can inspect, not a chat that smooths the friction away.

Break a question into agents only when one agent genuinely can't be one — when the access, dialect, or stance the work needs truly differ — then make them disagree on disk and force a framework to pick. SCOPE · personal → team → company: a single builder's research habit becomes the org's standing knowledge surface.

Three honest seams a single summary would have erased. The filesystem is the meeting room.
The mechanism · what the split actually buys

More agents isn't more intelligence.

Multi-agent has a glamour problem. It feels powerful — three minds, a swarm, an org chart of bots — and most builders reach for it because the shape looks serious, not because the work demanded it. Here's the unglamorous truth: a second agent that reads the same sources, speaks the same dialect, and holds the same stance as the first is not a colleague. It's overhead wearing a costume. You've doubled the coordination cost and bought nothing, because anything the pair could conclude, one good prompt could have concluded alone.

So the move starts with a refusal. Before you split anything, name the forcing axis: is it access (the agents literally reach different things — one sees the wiki, one the warehouse, one the open web), dialect (the sources don't speak the same language and shouldn't be normalised into one before you've looked), or stance (the answer needs a planner, an assumption-tester, and a reframer arguing, not one summary splitting the difference)? If you can't name which of the three is making one agent impossible, you don't have a split. You have one prompt cosplaying as three. Below: what the split buys is not more words — it's the seams a single summary papers over.

Process diagram · 01Same question. The split doesn't buy more text — it buys the three honest seams a single summary rounds away.

Sizing a market is the canonical case, because the answer is genuinely three answers in three dialects. There's the loud answer — press releases, analyst predictions, the numbers everyone repeats. There's the quiet answer — practitioner blogs, GitHub activity, what people say at conferences when the slides are off. And there's the academic answer — benchmarks, papers, the careful caveated version. Normalise those into one tidy figure before you've looked and you've thrown away exactly the disagreement that tells you what's real. Three retrievers, each fluent in one source's language, return non-comparable outputs by design. Don't let any of them average on the way in.

Faking the multi-agent shape with one prompt wearing three hats is the tell that you didn't need to split.

The upgrade · from a prompt in three hats to agents on disk

From the fake split to the split that bears load.

The brittle version is one chat thread doing all of it: a single agent prompted to "consider the market data, the practitioner view, and the academic literature" — three hats, one head, one transcript that quietly reconciles everything as it goes. It looks like multi-agent. It behaves like a summary. The load-bearing version gives each dialect its own agent and its own file — parallel sessions on a shared folder, or subagents inside one session; different shapes, same territory — and then makes a fourth move do the work the others can't: a framework that forces the question "where do these disagree?" before a single sentence of synthesis. Below: three hats writing to one chat on the left, three agents writing to three files on the right.

Process diagram · 02One head in three hats reconciles; three agents on three files, under a framework, are forced to show where they disagree.

A word on that framework, because it's the step most people skip and the one that decides whether the whole thing was worth the coordination cost. A synthesiser left un-prompted does what any model does at a fork: it rounds the corner and makes peace. Hand it three conflicting files and no spine, and it will produce a fluent, reasonable, utterly beige reconciliation — the very thing you split to avoid. Give it a framework — a strategy kernel by default, swap a stance if your challenge fits another (the default trio below is a starting point, not the only correct configuration) — and it stops averaging and starts picking. The framework is the synthesiser's spine. Without one, you've built an expensive way to get the single-agent answer back.

The compounding loop · what changes between passes

Next split starts from earned rules, not defaults.

The first time you split a question, you're guessing at the division of labour. By the third time, you shouldn't be. The artefact that carries the learning forward is a root ./CLAUDE.md that governs how the agents divide the work — and in the review after each run, you sharpen it from the four agent prompts and the retrieval files: this zone was noise, that stance was redundant, the framework needed a sharper "show me the seam" instruction. Each pass the rules file gets visibly richer, and the next question's split starts from earned division-of-work rules instead of a blank guess. Below: the loop, with the rules file densifying across passes.

Process diagram · 03The division-of-work file compounds. The first split is a guess; by the third the rules carry what earned its keep — and a teammate inherits it.
What "Test" actually means · in practice

The split earned its keep if the seam shows.

Here's the test, and it's harsher than "looks thorough." The answer has to be specific enough to bring forward and its uncertainty has to be plain enough to inspect — and a reader has to be able to see where the agents disagreed, because the synthesiser picked a direction instead of averaging the three into a hedge. Then the negative test, which most work fails — and that failing is the point. If you can't name which of access, dialect, or stance forced the split, or if one good prompt would have produced the same answer, you didn't need to split. You added coordination cost for nothing. Most work lives on that side of the line; the discipline is learning the move and respecting the default.

Use when

One agent can't sensibly cover the access, dialect, or stance the work needs — and you can name which of the three is forcing your hand. Can't name one? Keep the single agent.

Build

Parallel retrieval + framework-shaped synthesis: one file per source zone on disk, a synthesiser briefing carrying a framework, and a root rules file that compounds.

Test

Specific enough to bring forward, gaps plain to inspect, the seam shows.
Not merely "looks thorough."

Core moves

The action, in sequence

The first move is a refusal — it kills the splits that earn nothing.
1

Name the forcing axis

Access, dialect, or stance? Can't name one — don't split.

2

Split by source zone

One dialect per retriever. Non-comparable by design.

3

Write to files, not chat

The filesystem is the meeting room. One file per zone.

4

Run distinct stances

Default trio: planner · assumption-tester · reframer — swap one if your challenge fits another.

5

Force disagreement

A framework, or it averages. "Show me where these disagree."

question splits→retrievers write files→framework picks→seam audit sharpens the rules→repeat

Then it's a system, not a one-off: the next split starts from earned division-of-work rules. The same source-zone split that answered your question once becomes a running capability a colleague reads from.

Monday move: take one question you keep getting beige back on. Write down which ONE of access / dialect / stance makes it hard — if you genuinely can't, stop, keep the single agent, you just saved the coordination cost. Two sessions on one folder · each pointed at a different source zone · write to two files before anything synthesises · no fourth agent, no framework yet. No platform, budget, or sign-off — multiple sessions on a working directory already run.

Why
The principle

The filesystem is the meeting room. Parallel minds coordinate through files you can inspect — not a chat that smooths the friction away.

"Three agents don't make you smarter. Three different kinds of access, dialect, or stance do — and if you can't name which, you've hired three of the same agent."

More agents is not more intelligence; it's more access, more dialect, more stance — and only when those genuinely differ. The counterintuitive part is that the move which earns its keep is most often the refusal to split: most builders reach for multi-agent because it feels powerful, and most of the time one good prompt would have done it cheaper. When the split is real, the danger moves to the seams — conflicts get dropped, dialects clash, the synthesiser rounds everything into beige. The whole skill is watching where the pieces meet.

And the synthesiser needs a framework precisely because, left alone, a model's default at a disagreement is to round the corner and make peace. A framework forces it to choose. That is why the coordination happens on disk and not in a chat: a chat thread is built to reconcile, and reconciliation is exactly the friction you most need to see.

Most work doesn't need the split. Learn the move; respect the default.
The Work
Recipe · business lane · The Work

The validation gate

The principle: Hybrid beats autonomous — the move that scales is not "remove the human," it's "put the human in the one place that matters."

Find the irreversibility line in any workflow. Let the agent run free up to it. Put a human exactly on the step that can't be undone — and only there.

Personally it's the discipline that lets you ship an agent without betting what you can't take back; at company scope it's the architecture that decides where autonomy is allowed to touch the irreversible — the org-level guardrail every customer-facing, money-moving, data-touching deployment composes against, and the move that turns "should we automate this?" from a vibe into a placed gate.

The gate goes where the action can't be taken back — nowhere else.
The mechanism · reversibility, not capability

The agent is good enough. The architecture isn't.

Here is the counterintuitive thing. The named reversals — Zillow's algorithmic home-buying programme, Arup's fraudulent wire transfer, Air Canada's tribunal-enforced halluci­nated fare policy — are examples drawn from a convergence finding (15+ independent signals across 10 domains, assembled March 2026; practitioner reports, vendor reversals, consumer studies, analyst predictions). They are not proof on their own; the evidence is the convergence. What they share is not that the AI was unusually bad. It's that a consequential action reached the world with no human checkpoint before it. The 5% error rate that's acceptable on a reversible step is catastrophic when the step is "wire $25 million" or "update 483,000 patient records." Same accuracy, different consequence. The gate placement — not the model version — is the difference between a draft and a disaster.

There is also a compounding trap hiding in the chain. An illustrative calculation: assume 85% per-step accuracy — a chosen example rate, not a measured benchmark; the point is that errors multiply. On a 10-step autonomous chain, that's roughly 0.85^10 ≈ 20% end-to-end success. The long autonomous workflow fails not because any single model is weak but because accuracy degrades down a chain like compound interest in reverse. Customer-service deployments that perform well typically run 2–3 steps per interaction. Chain length and gate placement are the same design problem.

Process diagram · 01Gate placed after the irreversible step: the 5% lands where you can't take it back. Gate placed on the irreversible step: the same 5% is caught before it reaches the world. Same agent, same accuracy — the placement is the design.

The failure pattern in the convergence finding has a consistent shape: teams reach for full autonomy at the exact point it's most dangerous. A pilot succeeds at low volume. The plan is to crank the volume. The approval step that made the pilot safe quietly disappears — "that was just for the pilot" — and the first high-volume incident is not a technical failure, it's a governance one. Volume didn't change the agent's accuracy. It multiplied the exposure. The gate was the only thing standing between the model's occasional errors and consequences the organisation couldn't absorb.

Counter-evidence is real and must travel with the claim: a minority of practitioners (around 22% in one practitioner survey) report full-replacement success in bounded, well-scoped domains.
